stem: Under the bona fide needs rule, an annual appropriation such as one-year O&M may be obligated only for what?

options.text: A legitimate need that arises during the fiscal year for which the appropriation was made
options.why: That is the rule itself: a fiscal year's appropriation is obligated only to meet a bona fide need arising in (or sometimes before) the year for which it was appropriated.

options.text: Any need the agency can document at any point during the five-year expired period
options.why: The five-year window after expiration is only for adjusting and liquidating prior obligations, not for meeting new needs.

options.text: Any need, so long as the contract is awarded before 30 September
options.why: Award date alone does not cure a bad need; the need itself must arise in the period of availability.

options.text: Next fiscal year's requirements, whenever the current year has fall-out funds available
options.why: Using this year's funds for next year's requirements is exactly what the rule forbids.

cite: 31 U.S.C. 1502(a) (statute unchanged by the RFO)

stem: A customer submits a requirement above the simplified acquisition threshold and insists only one source can meet it. After market research still supports one source, what document does the file require?

options.text: A written justification for other than full and open competition, approved at the level set by the approval table
options.why: Above the SAT the restriction on competition must be justified in writing and approved; below the SAT the file only has to document the decision that one source is available.

options.text: Nothing beyond the market research report, because the customer's sole-source letter already serves as the justification
options.why: A customer's assertion is an input to the justification, never a substitute for it.

options.text: A determination and findings signed by the requiring activity commander, who owns the sole-source requirement
options.why: The requiring activity owns the requirement but does not approve restrictions on competition; approval runs through the contracting chain at the level set by dollar value.

options.text: Only a memorandum for record, since a written justification is required only for sole-source actions above $10 million
options.why: The written justification requirement keys off the SAT, not $10 million; dollar value drives the approval level, not whether a justification exists.

stem: A sole-source action is justified on unusual and compelling urgency. What is true about publicizing that action?

options.text: No presolicitation synopsis is required, and the justification is made public within 30 days after award
options.why: Urgency is an exemption from the presolicitation notice, and the urgency justification is posted after award rather than with the solicitation.

options.text: The synopsis is still required so other sources can respond, but the justification never has to be posted
options.why: It is the reverse: urgency exempts the synopsis, and the justification still becomes publicly available after award.

options.text: Both the synopsis and the justification must be posted 15 days before the solicitation is issued
options.why: Nothing works this way: the presolicitation notice runs 15 days ahead of the solicitation on a normal action, but a justification is never posted before award, and urgency excuses the notice entirely.

options.text: Neither the synopsis nor the justification is ever required for an urgent action
options.why: The justification is still written, approved and ultimately made public; only the advance synopsis is excused.

cite: RFO FAR 6.103-2 (was FAR 6.302-2); RFO FAR 6.301 posting of the justification, 30 days for urgency (was FAR 6.305); RFO FAR 5.101(b) presolicitation notice exemptions (was FAR 5.202); 10 U.S.C. 3204, 41 U.S.C. 3304

stem: Contract types span a spectrum of cost responsibility. Which pairing correctly describes the two ends of that spectrum?

options.text: Firm-fixed-price puts full cost responsibility on the contractor; cost-plus-fixed-fee puts minimal responsibility on it, with a fixed fee
options.why: Those are the two poles of the range, with incentive arrangements tailored in between as performance uncertainty varies.

options.text: Cost-plus-fixed-fee places full cost responsibility on the contractor; firm-fixed-price places it on the Government, which pays any overrun
options.why: This inverts the spectrum; under FFP the contractor absorbs cost growth, including any overrun, not the Government.

options.text: Time-and-materials places full cost responsibility on the contractor; firm-fixed-price splits any cost growth equally between the two parties
options.why: T&M gives the contractor no positive incentive to control cost, and FFP is not a shared-risk arrangement.

options.text: Both ends carry identical cost risk; only the profit percentage the contractor may earn differs
options.why: Contract types differ precisely in the degree and timing of cost responsibility, not just in fee.

cite: RFO FAR part 16 (contract types); RFO FAR 15.404-1 (price analysis, was FAR 15.404-1(b))

stem: A noncommercial acquisition over the simplified acquisition threshold requires a presolicitation notice. How long must that notice be posted before the solicitation is issued?

options.text: 15 days
options.why: The presolicitation notice runs 15 days ahead of the solicitation for a noncommercial buy over the SAT; for commercial acquisitions a shorter period or the combined synopsis and solicitation may be used.

options.text: 30 days
options.why: Thirty days is commonly the minimum response time allowed for receipt of offers, not the synopsis-to-solicitation interval.

options.text: 10 days
options.why: Ten days is associated with protest timeliness, not with publicizing a presolicitation notice.

options.text: 45 days
options.why: No publicizing rule uses a 45-day presolicitation interval.

cite: RFO FAR 5.101 presolicitation notice, 15-day interval (was FAR 5.203(a)); exemptions at RFO FAR 5.101(b) (was FAR 5.202); commercial alternative at RFO FAR 12.202(b)

stem: Per the thresholds carried in the board study bank, a written acquisition plan is required for a services or production acquisition at what value?

options.text: $50 million or more for all years, or $25 million or more in any one fiscal year
options.why: Those are the production and services triggers in the bank answer, with development at a lower figure.

options.text: $10 million or more for all years, or $5 million or more in any one fiscal year
options.why: $10 million is the development trigger, not the all-years services or production figure.

options.text: Any acquisition above the simplified acquisition threshold
options.why: Acquisition planning is always performed, but the formal written plan triggers at the dollar levels above.

options.text: $100 million or more, with no separate single-year test
options.why: There is both an all-years test and a single-fiscal-year test, and neither is set at $100 million.

cite: RFO FAR 7.102; DFARS 207.103 (thresholds as stated in the bank answer; confirm current values with C&P); 10 U.S.C. 3453, 41 U.S.C. 3307

stem: Which of the following is a recognized market research technique?

options.text: Querying Government-wide databases of contracts and other instruments meant for use by multiple agencies
options.why: Reviewing existing multi-agency vehicles and other Government and commercial databases is on the standard list of techniques.

options.text: Asking the incumbent contractor to certify in writing that no other firm can perform the work
options.why: An incumbent's self-serving statement is not research; it is the assertion market research is supposed to test.

options.text: Relying on the requiring activity's preference memorandum in place of outside inquiry
options.why: Customer preference is neither a source of market data nor a substitute for contacting industry.

options.text: Waiting for offers on an unrestricted solicitation and treating the number and quality of responses as the research
options.why: Market research informs the strategy before solicitation; offers received afterward cannot shape the decisions already made.

cite: RFO FAR part 10 (market research; results documented in a manner suited to the acquisition's size and complexity)

stem: What criminal penalty attaches to a knowing and willful violation of the Antideficiency Act?

options.text: Up to two years imprisonment and a $5,000 fine
options.why: Those are the criminal penalties for a knowing and willful violation, on top of administrative discipline up to removal.

options.text: Up to five years imprisonment and a $10,000 fine
options.why: The figures are higher than the statute provides for this offense.

options.text: Automatic personal liability for the full contract value
options.why: Personal financial liability for the obligation is not the statutory criminal penalty, although discipline and referral can follow.

options.text: There is no criminal penalty; only administrative discipline applies
options.why: Administrative discipline is the usual outcome, but a knowing and willful violation carries criminal exposure as well.

cite: Antideficiency Act, 31 U.S.C. 1341, 1350 (statute unchanged by the RFO)

stem: An appropriation is described as expired. What can the contracting officer still do with it?

options.text: Adjust and liquidate prior obligations for five years, but record no new obligations
options.why: Expired funds remain available for disbursement and adjustment of prior obligations for five years and are cancelled at the end of the fifth full fiscal year after expiration.

options.text: Record new obligations for the same purpose for five more years, as long as the need is documented
options.why: New obligations end at expiration, however well the need is documented; only adjustments to prior obligations continue.

options.text: Nothing at all, because expired and cancelled mean the same thing once the fiscal year ends
options.why: Cancelled funds are unavailable for any purpose; expired funds still support adjustments and payments.

options.text: Transfer the unobligated balance to the current-year appropriation for reuse on new work
options.why: Moving expired balances into a current appropriation would be an improper augmentation.

cite: 31 U.S.C. 1552-1553 (account closing; statutes unchanged by the RFO)

stem: Where does the authority to include a particular provision or clause in a solicitation actually come from?

options.text: The prescription in parts 1 through 51 that says when it is required, required when applicable, or optional
options.why: Every part 52 provision and clause has a prescribing section, and the matrix sends the contracting officer back to that prescribing text when the matrix alone cannot answer the question.

options.text: The contract writing system's clause logic, which becomes the controlling authority once the system is approved
options.why: The writing system is a tool that only knows what it was told. Approving the system does not make it the authority; the regulation is.

options.text: The clause matrix alone, which is a complete and self-sufficient list
options.why: The matrix is an index; required-when-applicable and optional entries must be resolved against the prescription.

options.text: Part 52 itself, since each clause states its own applicability in the line printed just above the clause text
options.why: The line above each clause only points back to its prescribing section. The trigger for using the clause lives in that section, in parts 1 through 51.

cite: RFO FAR 52.101(e), 52.102, 52.104, 52.105 and subpart 52.3; DFARS part 252 and AFARS part 5152 matrices

stem: Why does the commerciality determination matter to the contracting officer?

options.text: It drives which contract types may be used and which provisions and clauses apply
options.why: A commercial determination routes the buy into the commercial part, which limits contract type and largely fixes the clause set.

options.text: It determines whether the action must be synopsized at all
options.why: Publicizing rules turn on dollar value and exemptions, not on commerciality.

options.text: It sets the warrant class required to sign the award
options.why: Warrant class is set by dollar value under Army warranting policy, not by commerciality.

options.text: It decides whether the requirement can be set aside for small business or must be open to all firms
options.why: Set-aside decisions turn on the reasonable expectation of offers from responsible small businesses, not on commerciality.

cite: RFO FAR part 12; RFO FAR 12.104 (contract type, was FAR 12.207); RFO FAR 12.205 (provisions and clauses, was FAR 12.301); DFARS subpart 212.1

stem: What is the essential difference between a Statement of Work and a Performance Work Statement?

options.text: A SOW prescribes the contractor's actions; a PWS describes the required outcome in measurable terms
options.why: That process-versus-outcome distinction is the whole point, and the PWS is preferred where variance in method carries no risk.

options.text: A SOW is used for services and a PWS is used for supplies
options.why: Both are work descriptions for services; the difference is how tightly the method is specified.

options.text: A PWS prescribes the process step by step, and a SOW states only the objective
options.why: This reverses the two; a document that states only the objective is a Statement of Objectives.

options.text: A SOW is mandatory above the simplified acquisition threshold, and a PWS is used below it
options.why: Neither document is tied to a dollar threshold; the choice depends on where the performance risk sits.

cite: RFO FAR part 37 (service contracting); PWS definition at RFO FAR 2.101

stem: When acquiring commercial products or services, which contract arrangement is prohibited?

options.text: Any cost-reimbursement contract or cost-type line item
options.why: Commercial acquisitions are limited to fixed-price arrangements, fixed-price with economic price adjustment, and time-and-materials or labor-hour; cost-type contracts and CLINs are not permitted.

options.text: Fixed-price with economic price adjustment based on a price index
options.why: FP-EPA, including an adjustment based on a price index, is expressly available for commercial buys and is part of the stated preference.

options.text: Time-and-materials or labor-hour, for commercial services
options.why: T&M and labor-hour are permitted for commercial services, subject to the required determination.

options.text: Firm-fixed-price
options.why: FFP is the preferred commercial contract type, not a prohibited one.

cite: RFO FAR 12.104 (was FAR 12.207)

stem: What distinguishes a commitment of funds from an obligation?

options.text: A commitment reserves funds for a purchase request; an obligation legally binds the Government to pay
options.why: Funds stay committed until the contract action creates the legal liability that obligates them.

options.text: A commitment legally binds the Government; an obligation is only an accounting reservation
options.why: This reverses the two; only the obligation creates the legal liability.

options.text: They are the same act, described by the resource manager and by the contracting officer in their own terms
options.why: They are sequential, distinct events, and treating them as one is how premature obligations happen.

options.text: A commitment is made after award; an obligation is made before the purchase request
options.why: The sequence is the opposite: purchase request and commitment first, then award and obligation.

cite: DoD FMR volume 3 (commitments and obligations); Antideficiency Act, 31 U.S.C. 1341

stem: A contracting officer uses the combined synopsis and solicitation procedure for a commercial acquisition. What is true about the solicitation document?

options.text: The synopsis and the solicitation are combined into one notice, and the SF 1449 is not used to issue it
options.why: The procedure exists to cut solicitation time by merging the two notices, and the standard form is not used for issuance.

options.text: The SF 1449 must still be issued separately as the solicitation document, with the notice pointing to it
options.why: Issuing the SF 1449 separately defeats the procedure; the combined notice is the solicitation.

options.text: The procedure eliminates any response time for offerors
options.why: A reasonable response time is still set, and trade-agreement minimums still apply where they attach.

options.text: The procedure may be used only at or below the micro-purchase threshold, so larger buys need a separate synopsis
options.why: There is no such ceiling; the procedure is available for commercial acquisitions generally, to cut the time from notice to award.

cite: RFO FAR 12.202(b) (was FAR 12.603); RFO FAR part 5

stem: A contract is terminated for default after the funds have expired. Under what conditions may the original funds be used for a replacement contract?

options.text: Good-faith original contract, a continuing bona fide need, the same size and scope, award without undue delay, and a new contractor
options.why: All five conditions must hold for the replacement-contract rule to let expired funds cover the reprocurement.

options.text: The need continues and the scope stays the same, but the replacement may go back to the same contractor if its price is lower
options.why: Award to a different contractor is one of the stated conditions; a lower price from the defaulted contractor does not meet it.

options.text: None: after the funds expire, they can pay only for work the defaulted contractor already delivered
options.why: Expired funds remain available to adjust prior obligations, and the replacement-contract rule is a recognized use of them.

options.text: The need continues and the award is prompt; the replacement may also expand scope as long as the total stays under the original ceiling
options.why: Same size and scope is a condition; expanding scope means a new need that current-year funds must cover, even under the old ceiling.

cite: GAO Principles of Federal Appropriations Law, replacement contract rule; 31 U.S.C. 1502

stem: Which of these is a recognized technique for early exchange of information with industry before receipt of proposals?

options.text: Issuing a draft request for proposals for industry comment
options.why: Draft RFPs sit alongside requests for information, presolicitation notices, sources sought, industry days, one-on-one meetings and presolicitation conferences on the recognized list.

options.text: Sharing the independent Government cost estimate with a preferred offeror
options.why: Releasing the IGCE to one firm is a procurement integrity problem, not an exchange technique.

options.text: Telling one vendor the evaluation weighting in advance of the solicitation
options.why: Selective disclosure of evaluation information destroys the level playing field the exchange rules protect.

options.text: Waiting until the competitive range is set and then holding discussions
options.why: That is a post-receipt activity, not an early exchange before proposals come in.

cite: RFO FAR 15.101 (early exchanges with industry; was FAR 15.201(c))

stem: Which activity is an inherently governmental function that may not be contracted out?

options.text: Exerting ultimate control over the collection, control or disbursement of Federal funds
options.why: Controlling the acquisition, use or disposition of Government property and the disbursement of Federal funds is squarely on the inherently governmental list.

options.text: Preparing a technical evaluation worksheet as an advisor under a properly structured non-personal services contract
options.why: Support of this kind can be contracted when it is advisory, safeguarded and the Government retains the decision.

options.text: Performing quality control on the contractor's own work
options.why: Contractor quality control is the contractor's responsibility; Government quality assurance is the surveillance function.

options.text: Drafting a first-cut performance work statement for Government review and adoption
options.why: Assistance in drafting is permissible when the Government reviews, edits and owns the final requirement.

cite: RFO FAR 2.101 (definition of inherently governmental function); RFO FAR subpart 37.3

stem: A vendor submits a quotation in response to an RFQ and the Government issues a purchase order. At what point does a binding contract exist?

options.text: When the supplier accepts the order, either in writing or by delivering or substantially performing
options.why: The quotation is not an offer and the purchase order is the Government's offer, so the supplier's acceptance is what forms the contract.

options.text: When the Government issues the purchase order, because the vendor's quotation was the offer it accepts
options.why: A quotation is not an offer and cannot be accepted by the Government to form a contract.

options.text: When the quotation is received and found acceptable by the contract specialist acting for the Government
options.why: Receipt and evaluation of a quote creates no obligation on either party, whoever reviews it.

options.text: When funds for the order are obligated in the accounting system and the order number is assigned to it
options.why: Recording an obligation and numbering the order are internal Government acts; contract formation depends on offer and acceptance.

cite: RFO FAR 12.201-1(b) (was FAR 13.004(a) and (b))

stem: What best describes a bridge contract, and why does OSD track them?

options.text: A justified sole-source action that keeps the current product or service until a late follow-on is awarded, losing competitive savings
options.why: Bridges are symptoms of late acquisition planning, and each one forgoes the savings a timely competition would have produced.

options.text: A competitive short-term contract awarded while a protest of the follow-on is pending; OSD tracks them to measure how protests delay awards
options.why: The defining feature is that it is non-competitive and requires a justification. OSD tracks bridges as lost competition, not as a protest statistic.

options.text: An option exercised beyond the contract's stated ordering period
options.why: An option cannot be exercised outside its terms; that lapse is one of the reasons a bridge becomes necessary.

options.text: Any modification that adds funding to an existing contract near the end of its period of performance
options.why: Funding actions within scope are not bridges, even near the end of performance.

cite: RFO FAR part 6 justifications (6.103, 6.104); RFO FAR 13.101(b); RFO FAR 8.4 limited sources; RFO FAR 16.507-6 exceptions to fair opportunity

stem: A construction solicitation will carry a brand-name specification supported by an approved justification. What must the contracting officer do with that justification?

options.text: Include it with the solicitation notice, redacted as necessary
options.why: When an acquisition contains brand-name specifications, the justification or supporting documentation is posted with the solicitation notice.

options.text: Retain it in the contract file only, releasing it after award on request
options.why: File retention is not enough; the brand-name justification is published with the solicitation notice.

options.text: Provide it only to offerors who submit a written request before the closing date
options.why: Posting is public, not on request, so that all potential offerors see the basis for the restriction.

options.text: Post it 30 days after award, as with an urgency justification
options.why: The 30-days-after-award posting belongs to unusual and compelling urgency; brand name posts with the solicitation.

cite: RFO FAR 5.201(c)(3) (was FAR 5.102(a)(6)); RFO FAR 6.103-1(d) (was FAR 6.302-1(c)); approval per RFO FAR 6.104

stem: An unrestricted solicitation was open at least 30 days and only one offer was received. What are the contracting officer's two permitted paths to a fair and reasonable price?

options.text: Determine by cost or price analysis that the price is fair and reasonable and that adequate competition or another exception exists, with approval above the contracting officer; or obtain cost or pricing data and negotiate
options.why: Those are the two alternatives under the DoD one-offer rule, and the determination route requires approval one level above the contracting officer.

options.text: Cancel the solicitation and resolicit with a longer response period, because a single offer can never be found fair and reasonable without a second offer to compare it against
options.why: One offer is not automatically unreasonable, and a longer response period is not required; the rules provide a path to award without cancelling.

options.text: Award at the offered price on the strength of adequate price competition alone, because the solicitation stayed open at least 30 days, with no further determination and no approval above the contracting officer
options.why: Keeping the solicitation open 30 days is a precondition, not a finding. The adequate-price-competition determination itself must be approved above the contracting officer.

options.text: Negotiate a price above the offered price to reflect the lack of competition
options.why: The negotiated price should not exceed the offered price.

cite: RFO DFARS 215.202-71(c) (was DFARS 215.371-3); RFO FAR 15.403-2(b) and (c) (was FAR 15.403-1(b) and (c)); RFO FAR 15.403-3 (was FAR 15.403-4)

stem: What is the relationship between consolidation and bundling?

options.text: Bundling is a kind of consolidation that pushes out small business; all bundling is consolidation, but not the reverse
options.why: Consolidation is combining previously separate requirements; bundling adds that the result is unsuitable for award to a small business that was doing or could do the work.

options.text: Consolidation is a kind of bundling that pushes out small business, so every consolidated requirement counts as bundled
options.why: This inverts the set relationship between the two terms.

options.text: They are interchangeable terms for combining requirements, one used by the small business office and one by contracting
options.why: They are not two names for one thing. Small business participation separates them, and only bundling turns on it.

options.text: Bundling applies only to supplies and consolidation only to services, so construction is outside both rules
options.why: Both concepts reach services, supplies and construction; for construction, consolidation can exist where two or more discrete sites are involved.

cite: RFO FAR 7.107-2 (consolidation and bundling policy; old FAR 7.107-2, 7.107-3 and 7.107-4 merged); notifications at RFO FAR 7.107-3 (was FAR 7.107-5); 15 U.S.C. 657q

stem: Under DoD policy, a fixed-price contract may be incrementally funded in which situation?

options.text: It is for severable services, lasts one year or less, and uses funds that are unexpired on the date they are obligated
options.why: That is the severable-services path; the alternative is a contract using funds from two or more fiscal years that is funded with R&D appropriations or where Congress has authorized incremental funding.

options.text: Any fixed-price contract may be incrementally funded whenever the customer's funding stream is sporadic and the contractor agrees
options.why: Fixed-price contracts must be fully funded except in the narrow cases the policy permits; contractor agreement does not create an exception.

options.text: It uses procurement appropriations and the program office promises the balance next year
options.why: Procurement-funded contracts are the classic full-funding case, and a promise of future funds does not make funds available.

options.text: It is for non-severable services spanning three fiscal years, funded one year at a time
options.why: A non-severable effort must be funded in full with funds available when the contract is executed.

cite: DFARS 232.702 and 232.703-1; FAR 52.232-22 Limitation of Funds (cost reimbursement); DFARS 252.232-7007 Limitation of Government's Obligation (fixed price)

stem: A product development team cannot settle a Performance Work Statement that industry can price. Which option actually shifts the drafting burden to industry?

options.text: Issue a Statement of Objectives and have offerors propose the PWS
options.why: A SOO states the desired outcomes and lets each offeror write the performance work statement it will be held to.

options.text: Issue a draft PWS for industry comment
options.why: A draft PWS improves the Government's document but leaves the Government as author.

options.text: Issue the whole draft solicitation for comment
options.why: Useful, and a real option, but again the Government keeps the pen.

options.text: Add a brand-name specification so offerors know exactly what to price
options.why: That restricts competition and does not solve an unclear requirement; it hides it.

cite: RFO FAR part 37 (performance-based acquisition); RFO FAR 15.101 (early exchanges with industry)

stem: Which determination is NOT among those the contracting officer must make before exercising an option?

options.text: That the contractor has agreed in writing to accept the option price
options.why: An option is a unilateral Government right exercisable at a price already set in the contract; contractor agreement is not a precondition.

options.text: That funds are available
options.why: Confirming availability of funds is a stated precondition to exercise.

options.text: That the option fulfills an existing Government requirement and is the most advantageous method of meeting it
options.why: Both the continuing requirement and the best-interest finding are required.

options.text: That the option was synopsized as required, unless exempt
options.why: Synopsis of the option, unless exempt, is one of the listed checks.

stem: Under RFO numbering, where do the seven statutory exceptions permitting other than full and open competition now appear?

options.text: RFO FAR 6.103-1 through 6.103-7
options.why: The old 6.302-1 through 6.302-7 series renumbered one for one into 6.103-1 through 6.103-7, with headings unchanged.

options.text: RFO FAR 6.302-1 through 6.302-7, unchanged by the overhaul
options.why: Those are the pre-overhaul numbers a board will expect a candidate to have updated.

options.text: RFO FAR 6.104-1 through 6.104-7
options.why: 6.104 covers justification content and approval, not the authorities themselves.

options.text: RFO FAR 13.101 through 13.107
options.why: Part 13 covers soliciting from a single source under simplified procedures, not the statutory exceptions.

stem: A customer insists on a specific manufacturer's vehicle. Which approach still provides for full and open competition?

options.text: A brand-name-or-equal description listing the salient characteristics an equal product must meet
options.why: Brand-name-or-equal descriptions let other products compete, so under the FAR they provide for full and open competition and need no part 6 justification. Know the DoD wrinkle: DFARS 211.204 still requires a justification and approval to use a brand-name-or-equal purchase description.

options.text: A brand-name-only description, because the number of dealers solicited is what decides whether competition is full and open
options.why: A brand-name-only description does not provide for full and open competition, however many sources or dealers are solicited.

options.text: A brand-name-only description supported by the customer's standardization preference memo for its vehicle fleet
options.why: Preference or habit is not a justification; a genuine standardization or interoperability case still requires a written, approved justification.

options.text: A sole-source award below the simplified acquisition threshold, which needs no documentation in the file
options.why: A sole-source award does not provide for full and open competition, and even below the SAT the decision to restrict competition must be documented in the file.

cite: RFO FAR 6.103-1(d) (was FAR 6.302-1(c)); RFO FAR 11.204 (items peculiar to one manufacturer, was FAR 11.105; old FAR 11.104 brand-name-or-equal guidance moved to FAR Companion FC 11.204); DFARS 211.204 (DoD J&A for brand name or equal, was DFARS 211.104); RFO FAR 12.102 for commercial; RFO FAR 10.001

stem: Beyond the FAR conditions, what additional verification does DoD require before exercising an option?

options.text: Check SPRS (the Supplier Performance Risk System) for the required NIST SP 800-171 score and a current CMMC certificate at the contract's level
options.why: The DoD supplement adds the SPRS checks along with confirming an active SAM registration and accurate unique entity identifier, CAGE code, name and address in the contract.

options.text: Obtain a new determination of responsibility, signed by the head of the contracting activity and based on a fresh pre-award survey of the contractor
options.why: No HCA responsibility determination or new pre-award survey is required to exercise an option.

options.text: Obtain updated certified cost or pricing data for every option over the certified data threshold, even though the option price was set at the award
options.why: An option exercised at the price set at award needs no new certified cost or pricing data, whatever its value.

options.text: Re-synopsize the requirement as a new acquisition
options.why: The option only has to have been synopsized as required in the original competition, unless exempt.

stem: Which set names the three fiscal law checks a contracting officer makes before obligating funds?

options.text: The Antideficiency Act, the bona fide need rule, and the Purpose Statute
options.why: Those three, covering amount, time and purpose, are the standard pre-obligation checks.

options.text: The Antideficiency Act, the Contract Disputes Act, and the Prompt Payment Act
options.why: The Contract Disputes Act and Prompt Payment Act govern claims and payment timing, not the legality of the obligation.

options.text: The Competition in Contracting Act, the Truthful Cost or Pricing Data statute, and the bona fide need rule
options.why: The first two are procurement statutes, not appropriations constraints.

options.text: The Miscellaneous Receipts Statute, the Economy Act, and the Prompt Payment Act
options.why: These matter in specific situations but are not the three basic pre-obligation checks.

cite: 31 U.S.C. 1341 (Antideficiency Act); 31 U.S.C. 1502 (bona fide need); 31 U.S.C. 1301(a) (Purpose Statute)

stem: The contract required options to be exercised by 1 October. On 5 October the contracting officer realizes the option was never exercised, and the need continues. What is the correct action?

options.text: Treat the contract as expired, cover the gap with a new justified sole-source action, and start the competition now
options.why: An option not exercised within the time the contract specifies cannot be exercised late, so a bridge is a new contract action supported by a justification, not an option.

options.text: Issue the option modification dated 30 September to preserve continuity
options.why: Backdating a modification is falsification of the record, not a remedy.

options.text: Exercise the option now with a bilateral modification, since the contractor is willing and the price is unchanged
options.why: Contractor willingness, even in a bilateral modification, cannot revive an option whose exercise period has passed; any continued work is an unauthorized commitment requiring ratification.

options.text: Let the contractor keep working while a replacement is competed, then pay for the gap on the old contract
options.why: Work directed without a contract is an unauthorized commitment and must go to ratification, not quiet payment.

stem: What is the difference between the simplified acquisition threshold and simplified acquisition procedures?

options.text: The SAT is a dollar threshold set in the FAR definitions; SAP are the streamlined procedures used for buys within it
options.why: One is a number that triggers rules, the other is a set of streamlined procedures; mixing them up is a common board stumble.

options.text: They are the same thing expressed two ways, one in the definitions and one in part 13
options.why: A threshold and a procedure set are different concepts, and several rules key off the threshold without invoking the procedures.

options.text: The SAT applies only inside the United States; SAP applies only outside it, under contingency authority
options.why: Both apply worldwide, though certain contingency determinations raise the threshold for acquisitions performed outside the United States.

options.text: The SAT governs commercial buys and SAP governs noncommercial buys, so each one carries its own separate dollar ceiling
options.why: The threshold applies to both; under the overhaul the commercial streamlined authority sits in the commercial part while part 13 covers noncommercial buys.

cite: RFO FAR 2.101 (definition of simplified acquisition threshold); RFO FAR part 13; RFO FAR 12.201-1 (commercial simplified procedures, was FAR subpart 13.5)

stem: What distinguishes a delivery order from a task order?

options.text: A delivery order is for supplies; a task order is for the performance of services
options.why: The distinction is simply what is being ordered under the vehicle.

options.text: A delivery order is placed under an IDIQ; a task order is placed under a BPA
options.why: Both order types can be placed under indefinite-delivery vehicles; the contract type is not the distinction.

options.text: A delivery order is competitive; a task order is sole source
options.why: Competition requirements apply to orders of either kind, chiefly through fair opportunity.

options.text: A delivery order obligates funds; a task order only commits them
options.why: Both are contract actions that obligate funds when issued.

cite: RFO FAR 2.101 (definitions of delivery order and task order); RFO FAR subpart 16.5

stem: A customer's Commander offers to certify in writing that funds will be available so a year-end purchase can be awarded now. How does the contracting officer respond?

options.text: Decline; the resource manager certifies funds, and awarding without available funds risks an Antideficiency Act violation
options.why: Command emphasis is not a funds certification, and obligating in advance of an appropriation is a classic ADA violation.

options.text: Accept the Commander's written certification, since a general officer's signature outranks the resource manager's on funding matters
options.why: Authority to certify funds is a comptroller function, not a matter of rank.

options.text: Award the contract now, put the Commander's memo in the file, and record the obligation once the new year's funds come in
options.why: That is obligating in advance of an appropriation, the precise act the statute forbids; a memo in the file does not change that.

options.text: Award with a subject-to-availability-of-funds clause on a supply requirement in the current fiscal year, then fund it in October
options.why: That clause is narrowly available and does not exist to paper over funds that are simply not there yet for this buy.

cite: Antideficiency Act, 31 U.S.C. 1341; RFO FAR 32.7 (contract funding)

stem: An offeror asks for a letter saying award is imminent so it can lock in a material price break before 1 October funds arrive. What should the contracting officer do?

options.text: Refuse, because authorizing spending before funds are available creates Antideficiency Act exposure
options.why: A letter that induces the contractor to incur cost in reliance on a future award is the Government committing itself without an appropriation.

options.text: Issue the letter but state that it is not a contract and creates no obligation, which removes all risk
options.why: A disclaimer does not cure the substance if the letter is written to make the contractor spend money on the Government's expectation.

options.text: Issue the letter if the customer's leadership directs it in writing and the resource manager is informed
options.why: Customer direction cannot authorize an act outside the contracting officer's fiscal authority, and informing the resource manager does not create funds.

options.text: Issue the letter because the savings benefit the Government
options.why: A good price does not create funding authority; the savings can be pursued after award with current funds.

cite: Antideficiency Act, 31 U.S.C. 1341; RFO FAR 1.405 (ratification of unauthorized commitments, was FAR 1.602-3)

stem: Appropriated funds are subject to which three basic fiscal constraints?

options.text: Purpose, time and amount
options.why: Purpose limits what the money buys, time limits when the need must arise and the funds are available, and amount caps obligations at the appropriation.

options.text: Purpose, priority and appropriation
options.why: Priority is not a fiscal constraint, and appropriation is the source rather than a limit.

options.text: Time, amount and competition
options.why: Competition is a procurement requirement under a different body of law.

options.text: Purpose, amount and contract type
options.why: Contract type is an acquisition strategy choice, not an appropriations constraint.

cite: 31 U.S.C. 1301(a) (purpose); 31 U.S.C. 1502 (time); 31 U.S.C. 1341 (amount)

stem: An unsolicited proposal receives a favorable comprehensive evaluation. What does that mean for competition?

options.text: Full and open competition is still required unless an approved justification supports a sole-source award
options.why: A favorable evaluation is not an award authority; a restriction on competition still needs its own justification and approval.

options.text: A favorable evaluation is itself the authority to award sole source
options.why: The evaluation establishes technical merit, not a statutory exception to competition.

options.text: The proposal must be synopsized and competed with no exception available
options.why: An exception is available, but only through a justification approved at the required level.

options.text: The submitter is entitled to the award because it invested its own time and money in a unique and innovative idea
options.why: Offeror investment creates no entitlement to a contract, even for a unique and innovative idea.

cite: RFO FAR 15.506 (was FAR 15.607); RFO FAR 6.103-1(c) and 6.104

stem: Which statement correctly describes funding for a non-severable service?

options.text: The whole effort is funded with money available when the contract is made, and performance may cross fiscal years
options.why: A non-severable effort produces a single unified outcome that cannot be split by fiscal year, so the year of award funds all of it.

options.text: It is funded year by year as performance occurs, the same way severable services are funded
options.why: That is the severable rule, where the bona fide need generally arises in the year the services are performed.

options.text: It may not cross fiscal years at all, so the work must end by 30 September
options.why: Performance may cross years; what cannot be split is the funding.

options.text: It may be incrementally funded on a fixed-price contract with no further authority, one fiscal year at a time
options.why: Fixed-price incremental funding is limited to severable services within one year or where R&D funds or congressional authorization apply.

cite: 31 U.S.C. 1502; 10 U.S.C. 3133 (severable services contracts crossing fiscal years, up to one year)

stem: On 3 September of FY25, a PCO awards a contract with FY25 O&M funds for computers the contractor could deliver immediately, but delivery is deferred to early CY26 at the Government's request pending a new building. What is the fiscal problem?

options.text: A bona fide need violation: the need arises in the next fiscal year, and the lead-time exception does not apply
options.why: The lead-time exception covers delay driven by production and delivery realities, not delay the Government itself imposes.

options.text: There is no problem, because the contract was awarded and the funds were obligated within the period of availability
options.why: Award and obligation within the year do not validate a need that belongs to the next year.

options.text: There is no problem, because the lead-time exception covers any deferred delivery that the Government itself requests
options.why: The exception depends on when the contractor could actually deliver, which here was immediately; delay the Government asks for is not lead time.

options.text: It is a purpose violation, because O&M funds cannot buy computers meant for a new building that is still under construction
options.why: O&M is the right color of money for this buy, even for a new building; the defect is the year, not the purpose.

cite: 31 U.S.C. 1502(a) (bona fide need rule)

stem: What makes a services contract a personal services contract?

options.text: The Government supervises or controls contractor staff, or appears to, as if they were its own employees
options.why: The employer-employee appearance is the test, and such a contract circumvents the civil service laws, so it is permitted only when authorized by law and with the required approval.

options.text: The contract buys the services of named individuals, listed as key personnel, rather than the services of a firm
options.why: Key personnel requirements are common and do not by themselves create a personal services relationship.

options.text: The contractor's employees work on a Government installation, using Government desks, phones and computers
options.why: Place of performance and Government-furnished equipment do not decide the question; day-to-day direction does.

options.text: The contract is time-and-materials rather than firm-fixed-price
options.why: Contract type is unrelated to whether supervision creates an employer-employee appearance.

cite: RFO FAR 37.201-2(a) (retained RFO numbering; was FAR 37.104(c)); RFO FAR subpart 37.3

stem: Which combination is required for a contract to be performance based?

options.text: A performance work statement with measurable outcomes, a surveillance plan, price or fee reductions for poor work, and incentives
options.why: All four elements are needed; a PWS alone does not make an acquisition performance based.

options.text: A performance work statement alone, written in clear and objective terms, with the method of performance left up to the contractor
options.why: The measurement and consequence machinery is what makes it performance based.

options.text: A firm-fixed-price contract type with a cost-plus-award-fee option for any work the price does not cover
options.why: Contract type is a separate choice; performance-based methods can ride on more than one type, and no option structure makes a contract performance based.

options.text: A statement of objectives and a technical evaluation panel
options.why: A SOO is one way to develop the PWS, and an evaluation panel is a source selection mechanism, not a performance-based element.

cite: RFO FAR part 37 (performance-based acquisition); PWS definition at RFO FAR 2.101

stem: What must be obligated at the time an indefinite-quantity contract is awarded?

options.text: An amount sufficient to cover the minimum guarantee
options.why: The minimum guarantee is what gives the contract consideration, so it is obligated at award.

options.text: Nothing, because funds are obligated only when orders are placed
options.why: Orders are funded as issued, but the guaranteed minimum must be covered up front.

options.text: The full estimated ceiling value of the contract
options.why: The ceiling is a limit on ordering, not an obligation.

options.text: The value of the first year's anticipated orders
options.why: Anticipated order volume is a planning figure with no obligation effect.

cite: GAO B-318046; GAO Principles of Federal Appropriations Law, volume II, chapter 7; RFO FAR subpart 16.5

stem: Which describes a requirements contract, as opposed to the other indefinite-delivery types?

options.text: One contractor fills all of the designated activity's actual needs for the supplies or services during a set period
options.why: The definite-quantity type buys a set quantity for a fixed period, and the indefinite-quantity type buys an indefinite amount within stated minimum and maximum limits.

options.text: It provides for an indefinite quantity within stated minimum and maximum limits, with the minimum obligated at award
options.why: That is the indefinite-quantity type, including the obligated minimum.

options.text: It provides for delivery of a definite quantity over a fixed period, with each delivery scheduled by a separate order
options.why: That is the definite-quantity type.

options.text: It is a multiple-award vehicle under which awardees compete for each order
options.why: Multiple award with fair opportunity is a feature of indefinite-quantity vehicles, not the definition of a requirements contract.

cite: RFO FAR subpart 16.5 (indefinite-delivery contracts)

stem: Which of the following is a recognized exception to giving each awardee a fair opportunity to be considered for an order under a multiple-award contract?

options.text: The order is a logical follow-on to an earlier order on which all awardees had a fair opportunity
options.why: The recognized exceptions are urgency, only one awardee capable, logical follow-on, satisfying a minimum guarantee, a statute directing a specified source, and a small business set-aside of the order.

options.text: The incumbent awardee has performed well on earlier orders and the customer prefers continuity of the same team
options.why: Satisfaction with an incumbent is not an exception; that is the reasoning fair opportunity exists to test.

options.text: The order is below the estimated value used in the acquisition plan, so it is treated as a minor order
options.why: Planning estimates have no bearing on fair opportunity, and there is no minor-order exception.

options.text: The contracting officer documents that competing the order would take too much of the office's staff time
options.why: Workload is not urgency; the urgency exception requires that the delay would be unacceptable to the Government's need.

cite: RFO FAR 16.507-6(b) (was FAR 16.505(b)(2)); justification content at 16.507-6(d); DoD approval levels per DFARS 206.104-71

stem: A solicitation uses a brand-name-or-equal purchase description. What must the purchase description itself state, beyond the brand name and model?

options.text: The salient physical, functional or performance characteristics that an equal product must meet
options.why: Without stated salient characteristics, offerors cannot know what an equal product has to do, and the competition is illusory.

options.text: Nothing further, since equal products are self-evident from the brand name and model number
options.why: A bare brand name gives offerors no standard to propose against and effectively restricts competition.

options.text: The text of a justification approved at the head of the contracting activity level
options.why: A justification is a separate document, not part of the purchase description, and its approval level is set by dollar value rather than being the HCA in every case. Note for DoD: DFARS 211.204 does require a justification and approval to use a brand-name-or-equal description, and the documentation is posted with the notice for acquisitions over $25,000.

options.text: A determination that only one source is reasonably available
options.why: That determination supports soliciting a single source, which is the opposite of a brand-name-or-equal competition.

cite: RFO FAR 11.204 (items peculiar to one manufacturer; was FAR 11.105, with old FAR 11.104 brand-name-or-equal guidance moved to FAR Companion FC 11.204); RFO FAR 6.103-1(d); RFO FAR 5.201(c)(3) posting; DFARS 211.204 (was DFARS 211.104)

stem: The Source Selection Decision Document on a construction RFP is signed, but before the contracting officer signs the award you learn the Davis-Bacon wage determination has been modified. What must you do?

options.text: Amend the solicitation for all offerors in the competitive range with the new wage determination and let them revise their prices.
options.why: Wage rates must be current as of the day of contract award on a construction RFP, so the modification goes out by amendment and offerors get to reprice.

options.text: Award as evaluated and incorporate the modified wage determination by a unilateral administrative modification after award.
options.why: A wage determination change affects price, so it cannot be swept in as an administrative change after award without giving offerors the chance to reprice.

options.text: Ignore the modification because the wage determination locked in on the date the SSDD was signed.
options.why: The lock-in date for a construction RFP is the date of contract award, not the date the source selection decision was signed.

options.text: Cancel the solicitation and resolicit with the new wage determination.
options.why: Cancellation is a far more drastic step than the FAR requires; an amendment to the competitive range solves the problem.

cite: RFO FAR 22.403 (was FAR 22.404-6(c))

stem: A board member asks you to distinguish an offeror's experience from its past performance. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Experience is what the offeror has done, like a resume; past performance is how well it did it, like an appraisal.
options.why: This is the standard distinction: experience is the record of work performed, past performance is the quality of that performance.

options.text: Experience is how well the offeror performed, like an appraisal; past performance is the list of contracts it has held.
options.why: This reverses the two terms.

options.text: They are the same thing and are always evaluated as a single factor.
options.why: They are distinct concepts and may be evaluated as separate factors or subfactors.

options.text: Experience applies only to the prime contractor; past performance applies only to the subcontractors it proposes to use.
options.why: Both concepts can apply to the prime and to major subcontractors when the solicitation says so.

cite: Official CORB board answer, question bank Q0004 (no regulatory cite in the source)

stem: You have adequate price competition on a lowest price technically acceptable source selection. What does that mean for certified cost or pricing data?

options.text: You must not obtain certified cost or pricing data; comparing the competing prices shows reasonableness.
options.why: Once prices are based on adequate price competition the FAR prohibits obtaining certified cost or pricing data.

options.text: You must obtain certified cost or pricing data from the apparent awardee before award, as with any action over the threshold.
options.why: Adequate price competition is an exception to the requirement, not a trigger for it, whatever the dollar value.

options.text: You may obtain certified cost or pricing data at your discretion from any offeror you choose, if you document why.
options.why: The rule is a prohibition, not a matter of contracting officer discretion, once the exception applies; documenting a reason does not change that.

options.text: You must obtain certified cost or pricing data only from those offerors found technically unacceptable in the evaluation.
options.why: Certified data is never obtained on that basis, and unacceptable offerors are not in line for award.

cite: RFO FAR 15.403-2 (was FAR 15.403-1(b) and (c))

stem: In a competitive tradeoff, your cost realism analysis shows an offeror's proposed cost is understated. How does the result get used, depending on contract type?

options.text: On cost-type work you adjust to a most probable cost for the tradeoff; on fixed-price work the price stays, and the unrealism goes to risk or responsibility.
options.why: Realism adjustments produce a most probable cost only on cost-type work; a fixed-price offer stays at the offered price and the risk is reflected in the evaluation.

options.text: You adjust the evaluated price upward to the most probable cost on both cost-reimbursement and fixed-price contracts, and the SSA uses that figure.
options.why: The Government does not adjust a fixed-price offeror's price; the contractor bears that risk, so a most probable cost is used only on cost-type work.

options.text: You reject any offeror whose proposed cost is found unrealistic, regardless of contract type, because it shows that the offeror does not fully understand the work.
options.why: Unrealism is evaluated, not automatically disqualifying; rejection requires a basis stated in the solicitation, even when the cost suggests a weak understanding of the work.

options.text: Cost realism is the same analysis as price reasonableness, so one conclusion covers both.
options.why: Reasonableness asks whether the price is too high; realism asks whether the cost is too low for the offeror's own approach.

cite: RFO FAR 15.404-3 (cost realism), 15.404-1 (price analysis)

stem: A contractor submits a Certificate of Current Cost or Pricing Data. As of what date must the data be certified accurate, complete and current?

options.text: As of the date of price agreement, or an earlier agreed date as close as practicable to it.
options.why: That is the certification date the FAR certificate format requires, which is why a sweep is done before signature.

options.text: As of the date the final proposal revision was submitted to the Government for its evaluation.
options.why: Proposal submission, even of the final revision, usually comes before agreement on price, which is exactly why the sweep exists.

options.text: As of the date the contract is signed by both parties and distributed to the finance office.
options.why: Contract signature can follow agreement on price by weeks; the certificate is tied to agreement on price.

options.text: As of the end of the contractor's most recent fiscal year.
options.why: The certificate is event-driven, not tied to the contractor's accounting calendar.

cite: RFO FAR 15.403-4 (was FAR 15.406-2)

stem: Your project manager wants to add an information request to Section L that has no matching evaluation criterion in Section M. What is the right answer, and why?

options.text: Do not add it; each Section L request must match a Section M criterion, or using the information becomes an undisclosed criterion that loses protests.
options.why: GAO calls the use of an unstated criterion an undisclosed evaluation criterion, which is one of the most reliable ways to lose a protest.

options.text: Add it to Section L only; as long as the evaluators do not score it, no protest risk exists, and the project manager still gets the information it wants.
options.why: Once the information is in the proposal the risk is that it influences the decision, scored or not, and needless Section L content also burdens offerors.

options.text: Add it to Section M only and let offerors infer what to submit.
options.why: An evaluation factor with no corresponding instruction leaves offerors guessing and is equally defective.

options.text: Add it to Section L and collect it, then let the evaluation team decide after the proposals arrive whether it should count.
options.why: Deciding what matters after proposals arrive is the definition of an unstated criterion.

cite: RFO FAR 15.104 (evaluation factors and significant subfactors); official CORB board answer Q0064

stem: Which statement correctly describes the lowest price technically acceptable source selection process?

options.text: Award goes to the lowest evaluated price among the technically acceptable proposals, with no tradeoffs.
options.why: LPTA is used when the Government realizes no value from exceeding its minimum requirements, so there is nothing to trade.

options.text: Award goes to the lowest priced proposal, and technical acceptability is established after award during post-award orientation.
options.why: Technical acceptability is determined during evaluation; an unacceptable proposal is not eligible for award.

options.text: LPTA permits limited tradeoffs when a higher priced proposal is significantly better technically and the SSA documents why.
options.why: Permitting that tradeoff, documented or not, is the definition of the tradeoff process, not LPTA.

options.text: LPTA may be used only for construction and architect-engineer services, where the design sets the technical standard.
options.why: LPTA is typically used for clearly defined, low risk commercial or non-complex supplies and services, and A-E selection follows a different statutory process.

cite: RFO FAR 15.103-2 (was FAR 15.101-2)

stem: On a civil works construction project the proposals come in at double the independent Government estimate and the cost estimator stands by the IGE. What statutory limit is in play?

options.text: No civil works construction contract may be awarded at a price more than 25 percent above the Government estimate.
options.why: That statutory cost limitation for civil works contracts means award must be delayed until the pricing issue is resolved.

options.text: No construction contract of any kind may be awarded if the price exceeds the Government estimate by more than 10 percent.
options.why: Ten percent is not the civil works statutory limit, and the limit is not written for every kind of construction.

options.text: The contracting officer may award at any price once the SSA discounts the IGE in the decision document.
options.why: An SSA decision cannot waive a statutory cost limitation.

options.text: There is no statutory limit; the IGE is only an internal planning tool.
options.why: For civil works construction there is a statutory ceiling tied to the Government estimate.

cite: 33 U.S.C. 622 and 624; USACE UAI 36.205-100 (statutory cost limitations, civil works)

stem: You used competitive procedures, allowed 21 days for proposals, and received only one offer on a DoD requirement above the simplified acquisition threshold. What does the DoD one-offer rule require?

options.text: Consult the requiring activity on revising the requirement, then resolicit for at least 30 more days unless the HCA waives it.
options.why: Because the solicitation was open fewer than 30 days, the resolicitation requirement applies, and the waiver authority is the HCA and may not go below one level above the contracting officer.

options.text: Treat the single offer as adequate price competition, since the procedures were competitive, and award without further analysis.
options.why: One offer is not adequate price competition, even under competitive procedures, so the price must be proven by other means.

options.text: Cancel the requirement and convert it to a sole source justification.
options.why: A single response to a competitive solicitation does not convert the action to other than full and open competition.

options.text: Immediately require certified cost or pricing data from the single offeror, regardless of the value of the action or any exception.
options.why: Price analysis comes first, and certified data is required only if the action exceeds the certified cost or pricing data threshold with no exception.

cite: RFO DFARS 215.202-71 (was DFARS 215.371); DFARS provision 252.215-7007

stem: A firm that performs Government testing under a current contract wants to bid as a prime on a new source selection whose awardee will submit items to that same test contractor. What does the FAR require of you?

options.text: Identify and evaluate the potential organizational conflict of interest early, and avoid, neutralize or mitigate it before award, with advice from counsel and technical experts.
options.why: The contracting officer must address OCI early and recommend a course of action to the head of the contracting activity before the solicitation issues.

options.text: Automatically exclude the firm, because any current Government testing contract creates a disqualifying conflict.
options.why: A conflict must be analyzed and, where possible, avoided, neutralized or mitigated rather than assumed disqualifying.

options.text: Allow the firm to compete without further action, because organizational conflicts of interest apply only to advisory and assistance services.
options.why: OCI rules reach any situation where the nature of the work creates an actual or potential conflict, including testing and evaluation roles.

options.text: Refer the matter to the Small Business Administration for a certificate of competency determination.
options.why: A certificate of competency addresses responsibility of a small business, not an organizational conflict of interest.

cite: RFO FAR 9.502, 9.504 (organizational and consultant conflicts of interest)

stem: You received five proposals on a full and open competitive negotiated acquisition and have decided discussions are needed. What determines who is in the competitive range?

options.text: The most highly rated proposals, judged on all stated evaluation criteria, including cost or price.
options.why: The competitive range is built on the merits of each offer measured against the published evaluation factors, including price.

options.text: The three lowest priced proposals, since three is the standard size of a competitive range under the FAR.
options.why: There is no fixed number in the FAR or anywhere else; the range is determined by the merits of the proposals.

options.text: Every offeror that submitted a timely proposal, since excluding anyone before discussions is prohibited.
options.why: Offerors not among the most highly rated may be excluded, and they receive a preaward notice.

options.text: Only proposals that received no weaknesses or deficiencies of any kind in the initial technical evaluation.
options.why: Proposals with weaknesses or deficiencies can still be among the most highly rated, which is precisely why discussions are held.

cite: RFO FAR 15.206-1 (preaward notices; was FAR 15.503); RFO FAR 15.204

stem: Under the DoD limitations on the lowest price technically acceptable process, for which category is LPTA prohibited outright rather than merely discouraged?

options.text: Personal protective equipment and aviation critical safety items whose failure could cause death or injury.
options.why: The DFARS implementation of the statute prohibits LPTA for those items, as opposed to the avoid list.

options.text: Information technology services, cybersecurity, systems engineering and other knowledge-based professional services.
options.why: Those are on the avoid list, which is a strong caution rather than a prohibition.

options.text: Grounds maintenance and refuse collection services.
options.why: Those are classic appropriate LPTA candidates when the performance work statement is measurable.

options.text: Any acquisition of commercial products or commercial services.
options.why: Commercial buys to a clear specification are a common and permitted LPTA use.

cite: DFARS 215.103-2-70 (DoD Class Deviation 2026-O0048); 10 U.S.C. 3241; RFO FAR 15.103-2

stem: A commander wants a non-Government contractor employee, a unique technical expert, to chair the technical evaluation team and vote on the source selection board. Is that permissible?

options.text: No. Voting on a source selection board is an inherently governmental function, so a contractor employee may not do it.
options.why: Contracts may not be used for inherently governmental functions, and voting membership on a source selection board is specifically on that list.

options.text: Yes, if the contractor employee first signs a non-disclosure agreement and a conflict of interest certification for this source selection.
options.why: A non-disclosure agreement addresses information protection; it does not make an inherently governmental function contractable.

options.text: Yes, if the head of the contracting activity approves the appointment in writing before the technical evaluation starts.
options.why: No approval authority can delegate an inherently governmental function to a contractor, however early it is approved.

options.text: Yes, provided the contractor employee's firm is not competing on this acquisition.
options.why: Absence of a conflict does not change the inherently governmental character of the role.

cite: Official CORB board answer Q0133 (inherently governmental functions policy; source selection board voting membership)

stem: Which statement correctly describes communications, as distinct from clarifications and discussions, in a competitive negotiated acquisition?

options.text: Communications take place before the competitive range is set, and they may not let an offeror revise its proposal.
options.why: Communications exist to help decide who belongs in the competitive range, so proposal revisions are not permitted at that stage.

options.text: Communications occur after the competitive range is set and end with a final proposal revision.
options.why: That describes discussions, which are tailored to each offeror in the competitive range.

options.text: Communications are limited exchanges used when award without discussions is contemplated and can fix clerical errors.
options.why: That describes clarifications.

options.text: Communications must be conducted with every offeror that submitted a timely proposal.
options.why: Communications are targeted, primarily at offerors whose inclusion in or exclusion from the competitive range is uncertain or turns on past performance.

cite: RFO FAR 15.204 (exchanges with offerors after receipt of proposals; was FAR 15.306)

stem: In a tradeoff source selection, what must be true before you award to a higher priced, higher rated offeror?

options.text: The benefits of the higher priced proposal must merit the extra cost, and the tradeoff rationale must be documented.
options.why: That is the core tradeoff rule; an undocumented tradeoff is a protest exposure even when the decision is sound.

options.text: The higher priced proposal must be the highest technically rated proposal received.
options.why: A tradeoff permits award to other than the highest technically rated as well as other than the lowest priced offeror.

options.text: The price difference must be less than ten percent of the lowest evaluated price.
options.why: No percentage cap exists; the test is whether the benefits merit the additional cost.

options.text: The source selection authority must obtain approval from the head of the contracting activity for the price premium.
options.why: The SSA makes and documents the tradeoff decision; no separate HCA approval of the premium is required.

cite: RFO FAR 15.103-1 (tradeoff approach; was FAR 15.101-1); RFO FAR 15.205 (source selection decision)

stem: An unsuccessful offeror requests a postaward debriefing. Which of the following may you disclose?

options.text: The winner's overall evaluated cost or price and ratings, and the overall ranking of offerors if one was made.
options.why: Those summary results are expressly among the things a postaward debriefing includes.

options.text: A point-by-point comparison of the debriefed offeror's proposal with each of the other proposals the Government received.
options.why: Point-by-point comparisons with other proposals are specifically excluded from a debriefing.

options.text: The names and evaluated prices of the other unsuccessful offerors.
options.why: The identities and prices of other unsuccessful offerors are not disclosed.

options.text: The successful offeror's indirect cost rates, profit and cost breakdown, so the offeror can see exactly why it lost.
options.why: Confidential commercial and financial information such as rates, profit and cost breakdowns is withheld.

cite: RFO FAR 15.301 (postaward debriefing of offerors; was FAR 15.506)

stem: You are giving a required DoD postaward debriefing. What do the DFARS enhanced debriefing rules add?

options.text: Two business days for written questions, written answers within five business days, and the debriefing stays open until the answers are delivered.
options.why: The enhanced debriefing rule keeps the debriefing open until the written answers are delivered, which is what starts the protest stay clock.

options.text: The offeror gets ten calendar days to submit written questions, the Government has thirty days to answer, and the debriefing closes on the day it is held.
options.why: Those are not the enhanced debriefing timelines, and the debriefing does not close until the written answers are delivered.

options.text: The Government must disclose the unredacted source selection decision document to every debriefed offeror, whatever the contract value.
options.why: Disclosure of the source selection decision document is redacted and applies at specified dollar levels, not universally and not unredacted.

options.text: Written questions are permitted only at preaward debriefings.
options.why: The enhanced written question process attaches to required postaward debriefings.

cite: RFO DFARS 215.301-71 (enhanced postaward debriefing, was DFARS 215.506-70) and 215.301-70 (was DFARS 215.506), DoD Class Deviation 2026-O0048 Rev 1; RFO FAR 15.206-2 (preaward debriefing), 15.301-1 (postaward debriefing)

stem: A board member asks you to explain unbalanced pricing. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Some line item prices are significantly over or understated even though the total is acceptable; the offer may be rejected if that poses an unacceptable risk.
options.why: That is the definition and the remedy: unbalanced pricing raises performance risk and the risk of paying unreasonably high prices, and rejection is available.

options.text: It exists only when the total evaluated price exceeds the independent Government estimate.
options.why: Unbalanced pricing is about how the total is distributed across line items, and the total can look perfectly acceptable.

options.text: It exists whenever an offeror's total price differs from the other offerors' prices by more than twenty percent.
options.why: No percentage test defines unbalanced pricing; the analysis is line item by line item against the IGE, other offers and history.

options.text: It is a responsibility matter that must be referred to the Small Business Administration for a certificate of competency when the offeror is a small business.
options.why: Unbalanced pricing is a pricing and risk issue evaluated by the contracting officer, not a certificate of competency matter.

cite: RFO FAR 15.404-6 (unbalanced pricing; was FAR 15.404-1(g))

stem: An offeror timely submitted both a paper and an electronic copy of its proposal. The next day the electronic version proves unreadable. What is the correct action?

options.text: Notify the offeror at once and let it resubmit the unreadable part; it counts as received at the original time if sent as you direct.
options.why: The FAR expressly provides for notice and resubmission of unreadable electronic portions, and the original receipt time is preserved.

options.text: Reject the proposal as late, because a complete proposal was not received before closing.
options.why: The proposal was timely received; the unreadable portion has its own remedy and no offeror is harmed.

options.text: Evaluate the paper copy only and say nothing to the offeror, since silence protects the competition and keeps the original closing time firm.
options.why: The FAR requires that you notify the offeror; using the paper copy is permissible, but only after consultation and documentation.

options.text: Ask the offeror for a fresh electronic copy and evaluate whatever it sends, without comparing it to the paper copy that was already received.
options.why: You must confirm the resubmitted electronic version matches the paper version so the offeror gains no chance to revise.

cite: RFO FAR 15.108(c) (unreadable proposals; was FAR 15.207(c))

stem: You have a sole source proposal on an action that does not require submission of certified cost or pricing data. Which is an acceptable basis for determining the price fair and reasonable?

options.text: Price analysis against the Government estimate, prices paid before, market research, or published price lists.
options.why: These are recognized price analysis techniques and any of them, properly documented, can support a fair and reasonable determination.

options.text: The mere fact that the item appears in the offeror's published price list, which other customers also receive and use.
options.why: Inclusion of a price in a price list, catalog or advertisement does not, in and of itself, establish that the price is fair and reasonable, even if other customers see the same list.

options.text: The contractor's signed certification that its price is fair and reasonable and matches its best commercial price.
options.why: The determination is the contracting officer's, supported by analysis, not the offeror's assertion, however it is worded.

options.text: Cost analysis is always required on a sole source action regardless of dollar value, with a field pricing report.
options.why: Cost analysis is required when certified cost or pricing data is obtained or when price analysis will not establish reasonableness, not on every sole source action.

cite: RFO FAR 15.404-1 (price analysis techniques; was FAR 15.404-1(b))

stem: What distinguishes price analysis from cost analysis?

options.text: Price analysis judges the total price without its cost elements or profit; cost analysis reviews each cost element, including profit or fee.
options.why: Price analysis looks at the bottom line against outside data; cost analysis opens up the build-up.

options.text: Price analysis reviews each cost element and the profit; cost analysis looks only at the total price against outside data.
options.why: This reverses the two definitions.

options.text: Price analysis is used only on commercial items and cost analysis only on construction.
options.why: The choice turns on whether cost or pricing data is required and whether competition establishes reasonableness, not on those categories.

options.text: Price analysis relies on the offeror's own cost data, while cost analysis relies on data from sources other than the offeror, such as audits.
options.why: It is the other way around: price analysis is based essentially on data obtained from sources other than the prospective contractor.

cite: RFO FAR 15.404-1 (price analysis) and 15.404-2 (cost analysis)

stem: You are using sealed bidding and one bid shows line item prices that are materially unbalanced. What authority do you have?

options.text: You may reject the bid when you determine that the lack of balance poses an unacceptable risk to the Government.
options.why: Part 14 carries its own unbalanced pricing rule for rejection of individual bids; the test is the risk the lack of balance poses, not the fact that the bid is mathematically unbalanced.

options.text: You must award to the low bidder regardless, because sealed bidding has no unbalanced pricing rule.
options.why: Part 14 contains its own unbalanced pricing provision permitting rejection.
