options.text: Treat anything the FAR does not expressly authorize as prohibited, so that every one of your decisions stays well inside the four corners of the regulation.
options.why: A strategy in the Government's interest that is not prohibited by law, regulation or executive order is permissible; inventing prohibitions is its own error.

stem: When is a services acquisition strategy required in the Army, and when must it be approved?

options.text: When it meets the AFARS Appendix GG review thresholds, or at any value when designated special interest; approval comes before the final solicitation is released.
options.why: Appendix GG carries the review thresholds and delegations, special interest designation triggers a strategy at any value, and release follows approval.

options.text: Only when the total planned value exceeds the simplified acquisition threshold, and approval may come at any time before the contracting officer actually makes the award.
options.why: The trigger is the Army review thresholds rather than the simplified acquisition threshold, and approval precedes solicitation release, not award.

options.text: For every service acquisition, including each task order placed under a strategy that was already reviewed and approved.
options.why: Task orders issued consistent with the decision authority's conditions do not need a separate strategy of their own.

options.text: Only where a written acquisition plan is required, because the services strategy takes the place of that plan.
options.why: The written acquisition plan rules still apply on their own terms; the services strategy is a services-specific overlay, not a substitute.

cite: AFARS 5137.890-1; AFARS 5137.890-2; AFARS 5137.890-3; AFARS PGI 5137.890-4; AFARS Appendix GG; DoDI 5000.74; AR 70-13; RFO FAR 7.102; RFO FAR 37

stem: Who may waive the Defense Base Act for a country, and what conditions ride with the waiver?

options.text: Only the Secretary of Labor, on the agency head's recommendation; it never covers U.S. citizens, residents or U.S. hires, and it holds only if waived workers get local-law benefits.
options.why: The waiver authority sits with Labor, and both conditions travel with every waiver the Department grants.

options.text: The contracting officer may waive it for local national employees when the host nation runs its own compensation system, after checking with the Department of Labor district office.
options.why: No contracting officer and no contracting agency can waive the Act, even after consulting Labor; that authority belongs to the Secretary of Labor alone.

options.text: The head of the contracting activity may waive it on the contracting officer's request, and the waiver then covers every employee performing in that country, whatever their nationality.
options.why: The agency head only recommends, and no waiver ever covers U.S. citizens, U.S. residents or employees hired in the United States.

options.text: A waiver ends the contractor's obligation to carry any compensation coverage at all for the employees it covers.
options.why: Waived employees still have to receive local-law benefits, and the alternate clause keeps local-law and war-hazard coverage in place.

stem: A board member asks you to explain strategic sourcing. Which answer is correct?

options.text: Using spend data to combine common requirements, compete them once with full buying power, cut duplicate vehicles and track savings.
options.why: Strategic sourcing analyzes what the enterprise spends and turns that analysis into fewer, better-leveraged vehicles, which is where category management sits today.

options.text: It is selecting a single source for a requirement after market research shows that only one firm can meet the need at a fair and reasonable price.
options.why: That is a limited-source decision on one acquisition; strategic sourcing is an enterprise look at aggregate spend.

options.text: It is awarding each requirement separately to the lowest-priced offeror so that vehicles stay independent of one another and easy to replace.
options.why: Fragmenting buys is the opposite of the approach, which aggregates common requirements and cuts duplicate vehicles.

options.text: It is setting aside common commodity buys for small business so that the spend is spread across many more suppliers in more regions of the country.
options.why: Socioeconomic set-asides are a separate policy; strategic sourcing is about leveraging the Government's combined buying power.

cite: OMB M-19-13 (category management); RFO FAR 8.102, 8.103 and 8.104 (required sources and government-wide contracts); OFPP Memorandum, 29 Sep 2011 (business cases for certain interagency and agency-specific acquisitions); section 865, P.L. 110-417; RFO FAR 17.502-1(b)

stem: What is consolidation, and how does it differ from bundling?

options.text: Consolidation joins requirements from separate smaller contracts into one solicitation; bundling is the kind a small business cannot take, and it always needs the determination.
options.why: Consolidation is defined by combining previously separate requirements, while bundling adds the finding that a small business could not take the combined work.

options.text: Consolidation and bundling are two names for the same action, and each one needs a written determination only when the estimated value, with all options, is above $2 million in total.
options.why: Bundling is a narrower finding about suitability for small business, and it requires the determination at any dollar value.

options.text: Consolidation is combining separate line items inside one existing contract, so no determination is needed for it.
options.why: The term reaches requirements previously performed under separate contracts, and above $2 million it carries a written determination.

options.text: Consolidation is aligning the option periods of several contracts so they can be exercised on the same date.
options.why: Aligning option periods is contract administration; consolidation puts previously separate requirements into a single solicitation.

stem: How can consolidation benefit the Government, and what must the written determination show?

options.text: Savings, better quality, shorter cycle time and better terms, quantified from market research and shown to substantially exceed the alternatives.
options.why: Those are the benefits the regulation lists, and the determination stands or falls on quantified benefits measured against the alternatives.

options.text: Reduced administrative and personnel workload alone, which carries the determination when the office cannot run several source selections.
options.why: Administrative or personnel cost savings by themselves do not justify a consolidation unless the savings are substantial.

options.text: Increased small business participation, because one large contract gives small firms a larger subcontracting base to work from.
options.why: Consolidation generally narrows the field for small business, which is why the determination, the notifications and mitigation exist.

options.text: Benefits may be described qualitatively, because the substantial-benefit test applies only where the action is substantial bundling.
options.why: The benefits come out of market research as quantified figures, and the substantiality test applies to the consolidation determination itself.

stem: You have received the ABG7, all work is complete without deficiencies, and the customer has verified it. What is your next step toward closeout?

options.text: Get the final ABG8 and ABG9, confirm by voucher that they were paid, then deobligate leftovers on an ABG5a and process the 1594 and the PD2 closeout modification.
options.why: Closeout starts with the final invoices and proof of payment, and it matters because the unused funds only come back once the file is closed out.

options.text: Deobligate the remaining funds with an ABG5a right away, since the ABG7 already shows that the work is complete and the customer has verified it in writing on the ABG7.
options.why: The final ABG8 and ABG9 have to be requested and verified as paid before you know what funds are actually unused.

options.text: Close the action in PD2 and leave the residual funds on the contract until the appropriation itself cancels.
options.why: Returning unused funds is the reason closeout matters, so the residual is deobligated rather than left to expire on the contract.

options.text: Request a final ABG8 only, because the ABG9 covers administrative fees that are settled outside the contract, directly between the Bauamt and the local garrison staff.
options.why: Both final invoices are requested; the ABG9 for fees is part of the same closeout, not a separate settlement with the garrison.

cite: ABG-75 procedures (Germany); official CORB board answer Q0261 (confirm current local closeout steps with the 409th CSB)

stem: The Bauamt presents a request for equitable adjustment that is an interest claim for late payment. What steps do you take?

options.text: Find when DFAS got the invoice, count the days to payment, compute interest with the calculator, check funds on the contract, and process an ABG5.
options.why: The claim is evaluated by reconstructing the payment timeline, calculating the interest yourself, and then funding and processing it on the contract.

options.text: Deny the claim, since interest on a late payment is a DFAS matter that does not run against the contract.
options.why: The interest is calculated and paid on the contract through an ABG5, with additional funds requested if the contract cannot cover it.

options.text: Pay the figure the Bauamt calculated once counsel concurs, because the claimed amount is the amount due under the agreement's payment terms and no check is needed.
options.why: You establish the days yourself and compute the amount with the interest calculator rather than accepting the claimed figure, whatever the payment terms say.

options.text: Process the ABG5 for the claimed amount first and then look for funds if the contract does not cover it.
options.why: You assure the amount is available on the contract, requesting additional funds first if it is not, before processing the action.

cite: ABG-75 procedures (Germany); official CORB board answer Q0262 (confirm current local payment procedures with the 409th CSB)

stem: In ABG-75 construction, what do the KVM Bau, HU Bau and AFU Bau represent?

options.text: KVM Bau is the pre-concept design (about 15 percent), HU Bau the concept design (about 35 percent), and AFU the 100 percent design.
options.why: The three are successive design submissions, and the percentages are how a board expects the stages to be distinguished.

options.text: KVM Bau is the 35 percent concept design, HU Bau is the 15 percent pre-concept design, and the AFU is the Bauamt's final construction invoice.
options.why: The two design stages are reversed, and the AFU is the completed design rather than an invoice.

options.text: All three are Bauamt invoices, submitted at 15, 35 and 100 percent of construction completion for the contracting officer to approve.
options.why: They are design documentation milestones, not invoices measured against construction progress.

options.text: KVM Bau is the pre-concept design, HU Bau is the 100 percent design, and the AFU is the Government's acceptance document for the finished work.
options.why: HU Bau is the concept design at about 35 percent, and the AFU is the 100 percent design rather than an acceptance.

cite: ABG-75 procedures (Germany); official CORB board answer Q0263 (confirm current local practice with the 409th CSB)

stem: What fees is the U.S. Government required to pay under the ABG-75 agreement?

options.text: 5 percent of estimated construction cost for new work, 7 percent for repair work, and 0.5 percent for translation services.
options.why: Those are the VKE fees the Bauamt receives, with translation paid on top of the construction percentage.

options.text: 7 percent of estimated construction cost for new work and 5 percent for repair work, with translation included in the fee.
options.why: The percentages are reversed, and translation services carry their own separate half-percent fee.

options.text: A flat 5 percent of estimated construction cost for all work, new or repair, with no separate translation fee.
options.why: Repair work is at the higher 7 percent rate, and translation is charged separately at half a percent.

options.text: 10 percent of estimated construction cost for new work, with repair work and translation covered inside that fee.
options.why: No 10 percent fee exists here; new work is 5 percent, repair 7 percent, and translation is a separate 0.5 percent.

cite: ABG-75 agreement fees (VKE), Germany; official CORB board answer Q0264 (confirm current rates with the 409th CSB)

stem: What is the difference between an ABG8 and an ABG9?

options.text: The Bauamt invoices construction cost on an ABG8 and administrative fees on an ABG9.
options.why: Both are Bauamt invoices, separated by what they bill: the construction itself versus the fees.

options.text: The Bauamt invoices administrative fees on an ABG8 and construction cost on an ABG9.
options.why: That reverses the two forms; construction cost is billed on the ABG8.

options.text: The ABG8 is the Bauamt's design submission and the ABG9 is its final invoice.
options.why: Neither is a design submission; the design stages are the KVM, HU and AFU Bau.

options.text: The ABG8 obligates funds on the contract and the ABG9 deobligates whatever is unused.
options.why: Those are funding actions, and deobligation at closeout is done with an ABG5a.

cite: ABG-75 procedures (Germany); official CORB board answer Q0265 (confirm current local forms with the 409th CSB)

stem: How would you describe indirect contracting procedures?

options.text: German authorities plan, run and administer the work for the U.S. Forces, using their own staff and contracting with civilian firms.
options.why: Indirect means the host nation authority holds and administers the contract with the firm on the Government's behalf.

options.text: The U.S. contracting officer awards directly to the German construction firm while the Bauamt provides technical oversight and quality assurance.
options.why: A direct award by the contracting officer is exactly what indirect procedures are not; the German authorities contract with the firm.

options.text: A U.S. prime contractor subcontracts the work to local German firms with the contracting officer's consent.
options.why: That is ordinary subcontracting under a U.S. prime contract, not the arrangement these procedures describe.

options.text: The host nation funds the construction work and the U.S. Forces reimburse an agreed share after acceptance, under the cost-sharing terms of the agreement.
options.why: The procedures describe who plans, contracts and administers the work, not a cost-sharing arrangement.

cite: ABG-75 indirect contracting procedures (Germany); official CORB board answer Q0266

stem: What are the advantages and disadvantages of indirect procedures under ABG-75?

options.text: Pros: funds obligated before design is done, lower fees, a faster process and German expertise. Cons: unit price contracts needing close invoice checks, and late notice.
options.why: Those are the advantages and disadvantages in the answer, and the oversight burden is the price of the speed and the lower fees.

options.text: The advantage is that the contracting officer keeps direct privity with the construction firm, and the disadvantage is higher host nation fees.
options.why: Under indirect procedures the German authorities hold the contract with the firm, and their fees run lower than contracting the same services directly.

options.text: The advantage is firm-fixed pricing at award, and the disadvantage is a slower, more bureaucratic process than direct contracting.
options.why: Unit price contracts are the frequent arrangement, and the process is faster and less bureaucratic rather than slower.

options.text: The advantage is that a complete design is required before any funds are obligated, and the disadvantage is limited German technical expertise.
options.why: Being able to obligate construction funds before the design is complete is an advantage, and the Bauamt's technical knowledge is another.

cite: ABG-75 indirect contracting procedures (Germany); official CORB board answer Q0267 (confirm current local practice with the 409th CSB)

stem: What is the ABG3 form used for?

options.text: Ordering and approving design work step by step; the contracting officer signs it as an order under the agreement, and it can obligate design and construction funds together.
options.why: The ABG3 is the order that buys design in steps, and on an estimated basis it can obligate both design and construction funds at once.

options.text: Invoicing the Government for completed construction work once the customer has verified performance.
options.why: Construction cost is invoiced by the Bauamt on an ABG8, not ordered on an ABG3.

options.text: Deobligating the funds that remain unused at closeout, after the final ABG8 and ABG9 invoices have been received, paid and checked against the voucher record.
options.why: Deobligation at closeout is done with an ABG5a; the ABG3 puts work on order in the first place.

options.text: Recording the Bauamt's 100 percent design submission so the Government can accept the completed design.
options.why: The 100 percent design is the AFU; the ABG3 orders and approves the design work as it progresses.

cite: ABG-75 procedures (Germany); official CORB board answer Q0268 (confirm current local forms with the 409th CSB)

stem: Under ABG-75, what are the bid opening procedures as they concern the U.S. Forces?

options.text: The Forces get early notice of the date and place, may send a representative, and receive the invitation to tender with the proposed tenders.
options.why: Timely notice and the right to send a representative are the point, and furnishing the invitation with the tenders is what makes the notice timely.

options.text: The Forces conduct the bid opening themselves and the German authorities may send an observer to attend it.
options.why: That reverses the roles: the opening is the host nation's, and the Forces are the ones who may send a representative.

options.text: The Forces are told the outcome only after award, because the bid opening is a host nation function that they may not attend or observe at all.
options.why: The Forces are informed in advance of the date and place and may participate in the opening itself.

options.text: The Forces receive the invitation to tender only after bids are opened, to protect the integrity of the competition from any early disclosure.
options.why: The invitation is furnished at the same time as the proposed tenders precisely so notification arrives in good time.

cite: ABG-75 bid opening procedures (Germany); official CORB board answer Q0269 (confirm current local practice with the 409th CSB)

stem: What is the order of precedence in ABG-75 contracting?

options.text: The specifications in German, the special provisions, any supplementary technical specifications, the general technical specifications for construction contracts, then the general conditions of contract.
options.why: The German specifications govern first, and the documents descend from project-specific terms to the general conditions.

options.text: The general conditions of contract, the general technical specifications, any supplementary technical specifications, the special provisions, then the specifications in German.
options.why: That is the order inverted: the general conditions sit at the bottom of the order, not the top.

options.text: The special provisions, the specifications in German, the general technical specifications, any supplementary technical specifications, then the general conditions.
options.why: The specifications in German come ahead of the special provisions, and the supplementary specifications come ahead of the general ones.

options.text: The English translation of the specifications, the special provisions, the general conditions of contract, then the technical specifications.
options.why: The specifications in German are the governing document; a translation does not take their place in the order.

cite: ABG-75 order of precedence (Germany); official CORB board answer Q0270 (confirm current local practice with the 409th CSB)

stem: What are Project Specific Additional Services under ABG-75?

options.text: Project-specific studies: land, topographic, soil, hazardous material and structural surveys, an environmental compatibility survey and an energy use analysis.
options.why: These are project-specific studies of the site and the structure, ordered because that project needs them.

options.text: Warranty repairs the Bauamt performs on the completed facility after final acceptance of the construction work, billed to the project as additional services at cost.
options.why: The additional services are investigations that inform the project, not repair work performed after acceptance.

options.text: Translation of German documentation into English, which is billed to the Government at its own fee rate.
options.why: Translation is a separately priced fee item under the agreement rather than a project specific additional service.

options.text: Utility connection charges and forestry compensation that the Government pays as part of the project cost.
options.why: Those sit among the items the Government pays without a fee; they are not additional services ordered for the project.

cite: ABG-75 project specific additional services (Germany); official CORB board answer Q0271 (confirm current local practice with the 409th CSB)

stem: For which services does the U.S. Government pay no fees under ABG-75?

options.text: Tree cutting or reforestation, environmental or forestry compensation, utility connections, interest, and legal proceedings in or out of court.
options.why: Those costs are borne without the percentage fee that rides on construction and translation work.

options.text: New construction work, because under the agreement the percentage fee is charged only on repair work, and new work is billed at its actual cost.
options.why: New work carries a fee of its own; repair work simply carries a higher percentage.

options.text: Translation of German documentation into English, which the Bauamt provides to the Forces at no charge as part of its standard design and construction services.
options.why: Translation services carry their own separate fee percentage rather than being provided free.

options.text: Design work ordered in progressive steps, on the basis that it is covered by the construction fee.
options.why: Design ordered on an ABG3 is not among the items the answer lists as carrying no fee.

cite: ABG-75 fees (Germany); official CORB board answer Q0272 (confirm current local practice with the 409th CSB)

stem: A written solicitation will be issued for a commercial acquisition above the simplified acquisition threshold. Which procedure reduces the time required to solicit and award?

options.text: The combined synopsis/solicitation: one announcement that serves as both notice and solicitation.
options.why: One document does the work of two, and the announcement itself states that no separate written solicitation will be issued.

options.text: An oral solicitation confirmed in writing after award, which removes the publicizing requirement for the action.
options.why: The premise is a written solicitation, and publicizing applies regardless of how the solicitation is delivered.

options.text: Shortening the response time below the minimum set for acquisitions covered by a trade agreement, with a written justification.
options.why: Those minimum response periods still apply, justified or not; otherwise you set a time that gives offerors a reasonable opportunity to respond.

options.text: Issuing the solicitation on an SF 1449, which then serves as both the synopsis and the solicitation.
options.why: When the combined procedure is used, the SF 1449 is not the document that issues the solicitation.

cite: RFO FAR 12.202; RFO FAR 12.202(b); RFO FAR 5.201(c); RFO FAR 5.201(d)

stem: In August 2026 a requiring activity sends you a purchase request using FY26 O&M funds for a one-year janitorial contract to be performed 1 July 2027 through 30 June 2028, citing worries about next year's budget. What do you do?

options.text: Return it: janitorial work is severable, so the need arises when performed; explain why and ask for an FY27-funded request.
options.why: For severable services the bona fide need arises as the services are performed, not when the contract is awarded or the funds happen to be available.

options.text: Accept it, because the bona fide need arises when the contract is awarded and the funds were available and certified in FY26.
options.why: The award date does not fix the year of the need; for severable services the need follows performance.

options.text: Accept it, since a severable services contract may cross fiscal years for a period of up to twelve months.
options.why: This period of performance lies entirely in the following fiscal year, so it is an FY27 need and FY26 funds are not available for it.

options.text: Award with FY26 funds now and modify the contract later to replace them once the FY27 appropriation finally arrives in the fall.
options.why: The improper obligation happens at award, and planning a later swap does not make the original funding lawful.

stem: A customer needs about $40,000 of maintenance on power conditioners and says only the manufacturer can do the work because of proprietary information and specialized parts. How do you proceed?

options.text: Use simplified procedures: get the needs in writing, still do market research, document the single-source decision, and post on SAM.gov with the redacted justification.
options.why: At $40,000 the action sits above the micro-purchase threshold and below the SAT, so the restriction is documented under the simplified procedures and still publicized.

options.text: Prepare a justification for other than full and open competition and route it through the approval level set for this dollar value in the approval table.
options.why: The Part 6 justification and its approval tables apply above the simplified acquisition threshold, not to a $40,000 action.

options.text: Skip the market research and the notice, because the customer has already established that only one source can perform.
options.why: The customer's conclusion is not market research, and a sole source at this value is not exempt from publicizing.

options.text: Place it on the purchase card as a single-source buy, since the capable firm has already been identified.
options.why: The value is well above the micro-purchase threshold, so the purchase card is not the instrument for this action.

cite: RFO FAR 2.101 (micro-purchase threshold $15,000; SAT $350,000); RFO FAR 12.102(a); RFO FAR 13.101(b); RFO FAR 11.204 and DFARS 211.204; RFO FAR 6.001 and 6.103-1(d); RFO FAR 5.101 and 5.201(c)(3); RFO FAR 10.001

stem: A GPC cardholder needs 60 office chairs from one Korean vendor, quoted at about $19,500 delivered. She proposes buying 30 this week and 30 next week, or putting half on a colleague's card, since the limit is $15,000 and they are overseas. What do you tell the billing official?

options.text: Both are split purchases, over time and across cardholders, and Korea does not raise the $15,000 limit; send it to contracting for an order.
options.why: Sixty chairs from one vendor for one customer is a single requirement above the threshold, so it is bought on a contract action rather than carved up.

options.text: Thirty chairs in each of two weeks is acceptable, because each of those transactions stays under the micro-purchase threshold and has its own receipt.
options.why: Splitting a requirement over time is one of the defined forms of a split purchase, whatever each transaction totals or however it is receipted.

options.text: Putting half on a colleague's card is acceptable, because each cardholder stays within her own single-purchase limit.
options.why: Splitting among cardholders is equally a violation; the aggregate requirement is what the threshold measures.

options.text: Overseas cardholders may buy up to $40,000, so the full requirement fits on one card without splitting it.
options.why: The higher overseas figure applies only under a head-of-agency contingency or emergency determination, which office chairs do not have.

cite: RFO FAR 2.101; RFO FAR 12.001(d); RFO FAR 12.201-1; RFO FAR 13.001(c); AFARS 5113.270-90; AFARS Appendix EE; DoD Government Charge Card Guidebook

stem: A facility manager called a Korean HVAC firm directly over a weekend; it replaced two rooftop units at a child development center and invoiced about $46,000. The garrison commander offers to sign whatever is needed. What is this action, and who can ratify it?

options.text: An unauthorized commitment; the HCA may ratify, delegating no lower than the chief of the contracting office; confirm the official with the Chief, C&P.
options.why: The agreement is not binding only because the maker had no authority, and ratification authority runs through the contracting chain, not the garrison.

options.text: The garrison commander may ratify it by endorsing the invoice, since he commands the facility, controls the funds, and his staff accepted the finished work.
options.why: A commander's signature belongs on the endorsement of the facts, not on the obligation; he cannot ratify, even after his staff accepted the work.

options.text: It cannot be ratified at all because the vendor is not registered in SAM, so a claim is the vendor's only route.
options.why: Registration is a separate question with its own exceptions, and a claim is the path only if ratification is not granted.

options.text: Any contracting officer whose warrant covers the value may ratify it and issue the purchase order as a routine action, with a copy to the garrison commander.
options.why: Ratification is not a warrant function; the authority sits with the head of the contracting activity and its permitted delegation.

cite: RFO FAR 1.405; AFARS 5101.602-3; AFARS 5101.602-3-90; AFARS Appendix GG; 31 U.S.C. 1341; 31 U.S.C. 3702

stem: A Korean-national direct-hire contract specialist with six years of experience and a bachelor's degree from a Korean university asks to be warranted. Can a foreign local national hold an Army contracting warrant, and what documents the equivalence of her education?

options.text: Yes. The policy covers foreign local nationals, and an OCONUS HCA may recognize equivalent education in an FLN Validation Letter in VCE-Warrants.
options.why: The policy reaches foreign local nationals who need a warrant under Army authority, and the validation letter is what documents the equivalence.

options.text: No. A contracting warrant may be issued only to Department of the Army civilians and to military personnel.
options.why: The warranting policy expressly covers foreign local nationals who require a warrant under Army authority.

options.text: Yes, but only once she earns a degree from a U.S. accredited institution, since a degree from a foreign university cannot be recognized for a warrant.
options.why: The OCONUS head of contracting activity has authority to recognize equivalent education and training, which is the point of the validation letter.

options.text: Yes, and no education documentation is needed, because six years of contracting experience substitutes for the degree.
options.why: Above the simplified acquisition threshold the statutory qualifications include the degree, so the education still has to be addressed.

cite: Army Warranting Program Policy v12 (MAR 2026); DA memorandum, Contracting Validation for Foreign Local Nationals, Policy and Procedures (18 Nov 2022); 10 U.S.C. 1724; RFO DFARS 201.403-70; 411th CSB Warrant Process Workflow (Jul 2026); confirm the current validation letter template and routing with C&P

stem: A brigade S3 sends a $68,000 purchase request naming an individual interpreter who would work 0800 to 1700 in the S3 shop, take daily taskings from the S3, use a Government computer, attend staff meetings, and be rated by the S3. How do you handle it?

options.text: It is personal services as written, since the S3 would supervise her like an employee; use a nonpersonal services contract or a direct hire.
options.why: Relatively continuous Government supervision is the key indicator, and every feature of this request builds that relationship by design.

options.text: It is acceptable as requested, because the last interpreter was a contractor, that arrangement worked without any problem, and the S3 is satisfied.
options.why: Prior practice and customer satisfaction are not an authority; what governs is whether the Government supervises the contractor employee as if she were its own.

options.text: It is acceptable if the requiring activity certifies in writing that the need for the named individual is urgent and that no other interpreter is available.
options.why: A personal services contract overseas needs written approval from the head of the contracting activity with specific determinations, not a customer certification.

options.text: It is nonpersonal as long as the contract is firm-fixed-price and a COR is appointed to pass the daily taskings from the S3 to the interpreter.
options.why: Contract type and a COR do not cure continuous supervision; work is ordered through the contract rather than directed day to day.

cite: RFO FAR 37.201-1; RFO FAR 37.201-2(a) and (b); RFO FAR 37.202-1; RFO DFARS 237.201-70; RFO DFARS 237.876; 10 U.S.C. 129b(d); 5 U.S.C. 3109; DFARS PGI 201.404-70

stem: You hold a Class II $5 million warrant issued by the 411th CSB SCO and are placed under the operational control of a different ACC senior contracting official. That office tells you to apply for its own warrant and to sign a $7 million commercial services award. What is correct?

options.text: No new warrant is needed, since ACC officials must honor active ACC warrants, but a $5 million warrant cannot sign $7 million; seek an increase through your ADCON organization.
options.why: Reciprocity recognizes the existing warrant at its existing dollar value, and the warrant still has to cover the cumulative value of anything you sign.

options.text: Apply for the gaining official's warrant, since a warrant is only valid for actions of the organization whose official issued it.
options.why: Issuing a second warrant is the duplication reciprocity was written to prevent; the gaining official recognizes the warrant you hold.

options.text: Sign the award, because recognition by the gaining official carries whatever authority that office's actions require.
options.why: Warrants are recognized at their existing type and value, so recognition does not raise a $5 million warrant to cover $7 million.

options.text: The Air Force contracting officer detailed to the same office has her warrant transfer automatically under the same reciprocity rule, at its full value.
options.why: A warrant issued outside ACC is recognized only at the gaining official's discretion, and a new ACC warrant must still be issued, whatever its value.

cite: ACC Contracting Note 26-03 (Warrant Reciprocity Guidance, 12 May 2026); ACC Command Policy Memorandum, Warrant Reciprocity Policy (30 Mar 2026); Army-DAF Warrant Reciprocity MOA (1 Dec 2023); Army Warranting Program Policy v12 (MAR 2026); RFO FAR 1.402-1; 411th CSB Warrant Process Workflow (Jul 2026)

stem: A firm-fixed-price negotiation is proposed at $120 million and the two sides are $15 million apart. Your maximum position allows only $8 million of movement. The project manager asks you to offer the contractor a 50/50 split of the current positions to speed things up. What do you tell the project manager?

options.text: We do not split a gap this large: a $7.5 million move leaves only $500,000 of room, and if the contractor refuses, our credibility is gone.
options.why: Those are the three reasons the Government does not split at this magnitude: no room left to move, no credibility left, and nothing for management to adjust.

options.text: Offer the split, but tell the contractor we reserve the right to return to our previous position if it does not accept within the coming week.
options.why: Reserving that right is like telling a jury to ignore a statement; the contractor now knows we can reach the split figure and will negotiate from there.

options.text: Offer the split, because it is defensible as long as it stays inside the $8 million that the approved maximum position still allows us to move.
options.why: Fitting inside the maximum is not the test; a $7.5 million jump spends nearly all of the authorized movement in one step.

options.text: Tell the project manager the pace of the negotiation is his call, and make the offer this week to close it out.
options.why: Customer schedule pressure does not justify a bargaining move that surrenders the Government's position and the negotiating team's credibility.

cite: Official CORB board answer Q0065 (negotiation objective and Government maximum position; no regulatory cite in the source)

stem: After a claim accrues, how long does a contractor have to submit that claim in writing to the contracting officer for a decision?

options.text: Six years from accrual, unless the contract sets a shorter period, and the same limit applies to Government claims.
options.why: The Contract Disputes Act sets a six-year limit running from accrual, and it runs both ways.

options.text: Ninety days, the same period the contractor has to file an appeal with the Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals.
options.why: Ninety days is the window to appeal a contracting officer's final decision to the board, not the time to submit the claim.

options.text: Twelve months, matching the period for bringing an action at the Court of Federal Claims.
options.why: Twelve months is the period to go to the Court of Federal Claims after a final decision, not the submission limit.

options.text: Sixty days, the period in which the contracting officer must issue a decision on a certified claim.
options.why: Sixty days is the contracting officer's decision clock, not the contractor's filing limit.

stem: You are a contingency contracting officer. Units keep giving local vendors verbal direction before requirements reach you, and the commander wants everything immediately. How do you balance speed against discipline?

options.text: Use contingency thresholds and faster methods, but document every action and price, meet weekly with the J4 and S4s on requirements, and process the commitments for ratification.
options.why: The flexibilities speed up the method, not the record, and the weekly requirements sync is what gets the requirement to the KO before the vendor gets it.

options.text: Ratify the verbal orders after the fact but skip the written price determinations, since contingency flexibilities suspend the documentation requirements for the length of the deployment.
options.why: The contingency flexibilities raise thresholds and allow quicker methods; they do not remove the written determination or the price memo.

options.text: Let the units keep placing verbal orders and paper the files later at redeployment, when there is time to do it properly.
options.why: The protests and claims that follow a contingency come out of the files that were never built at the time.

options.text: Write one urgency justification broad enough to cover the whole deployment so individual actions need no separate support.
options.why: An urgency justification still has to be true for the action it supports; a blanket justification is not.

cite: RFO FAR 18.001; DFARS 218.7001-2; RFO FAR 1.405; RFO FAR 6.103-2; RFO FAR 9.104-1

stem: On a larger source selection, how does the Government develop its negotiation objective?

options.text: A team evaluates the proposal, technical evaluators on performance and cost/price evaluators on pricing, and both go into the approved prenegotiation memorandum.
options.why: That is the process: a team of evaluators, split technical and cost/price, whose results are captured in the prenegotiation memorandum and approved.

options.text: The contracting officer sets the objective alone from the independent government estimate, then briefs the entire evaluation team once that objective is approved.
options.why: The objective is built by the evaluation team, not by the contracting officer working from the estimate alone.

options.text: The technical evaluators price the proposal and the cost and price analysts judge whether the offeror can meet the requirement.
options.why: The roles are reversed: technical evaluators assess likelihood of performance, cost/price evaluators evaluate the pricing information.

options.text: The objective forms during negotiations out of the contractor's responses and is written up afterward in the price negotiation memorandum for the official contract file.
options.why: The objective is set and approved before negotiating; the record made afterward is a different document.

cite: Official CORB board answer Q0136 (Ch. 3, Negotiation Preparation, osd.mil)

stem: During evaluations on a services recompete, a technical evaluator wants to credit an offeror with a strength for a capability the RFP never asked for. What protects the integrity of the source selection?

options.text: Stop it: we evaluate only on the published factors, and if it matters we amend the RFP so all offerors can respond.
options.why: Crediting something never published is an unstated criterion and a sustainable protest; the cure is an amendment that lets everyone respond.

options.text: Allow the strength as long as the evaluation record explains in detail why the capability benefits the Government's mission.
options.why: Documenting an unstated criterion does not cure it; the criterion still was never published to the other offerors.

options.text: Carry it forward and let the source selection authority decide at the decision briefing whether it should count at all.
options.why: The SSA's comparative assessment rests on the stated criteria too, so passing the problem up does not fix it.

options.text: Raise it with that offeror in discussions so the capability is formally proposed in writing, then evaluate it as a strength.
options.why: Discussions cannot import a criterion the solicitation never stated, and raising it with one offeror is unequal treatment.

cite: RFO FAR 15.104; RFO FAR 15.202; RFO FAR 15.204; RFO FAR 15.205

stem: GAO's jurisdiction over protests of task and delivery orders is limited. Apart from the dollar threshold for Department of Defense orders, on what other basis may GAO hear an order protest?

options.text: That the contract action increases the scope, period, or maximum value of the contract under which the order is issued.
options.why: A protest that the action increases the scope, period or maximum value of the underlying contract may be heard regardless of the order's value.

options.text: That the order was placed without giving the multiple-award holders a fair opportunity to be considered.
options.why: A fair opportunity complaint is not by itself a jurisdictional basis; it still has to clear the order value threshold.

options.text: That the agency failed to give the postaward debriefing required on the order.
options.why: A debriefing failure is a procedural complaint, not an independent basis for jurisdiction over an order protest.

options.text: That the order was charged to the wrong appropriation or the wrong contract line item.
options.why: A fiscal or administrative error is not one of the grounds that opens GAO's door on an order.

cite: RFO FAR 16.508 (protests of orders; legacy FAR 16.505(a)(10))

stem: How does an Other Transaction differ from a FAR-based contract?

options.text: An OT is binding but is not a procurement contract, grant or cooperative agreement, so the FAR and procurement statutes apply only if written in.
options.why: That is the defining difference: the instrument sits outside the procurement framework, so CICA, the FAR, the Contract Disputes Act and the standard clause set reach it only by agreement.

options.text: An OT is a FAR contract issued under a class deviation that waives the clauses the agency chooses not to use.
options.why: An OT is not a procurement contract at all; it does not begin from the FAR and is not created by deviation.

options.text: An OT is a procurement contract awarded without competition, which is why only an agreements officer holding a special OT warrant may sign one for the Army.
options.why: Prototype OTs require competitive procedures to the maximum extent practicable, and the agreements officer signs because of the instrument, not a lack of competition.

options.text: Because the FAR does not apply, fiscal law and the procurement integrity rules do not reach an OT either.
options.why: Fiscal law, the bona fide need rule, ethics, procurement integrity and Army warrant limits all still apply to OTs.

cite: 10 U.S.C. 4021; 10 U.S.C. 4022; 31 U.S.C. 6303; DoD Other Transactions Guide (2023)

stem: What are a grants officer's responsibilities?

options.text: Effective use of awards made and run under law, Executive orders, regulation and DoD policy; funds available for obligation; and fair, impartial treatment of recipients.
options.why: Those are the three responsibilities the grants officer exercises wide latitude and judgment to carry out.

options.text: Ensuring every award is competed, priced with certified cost or pricing data, and administered under the standard FAR clause set.
options.why: Assistance awards are not FAR procurements, so certified cost or pricing data and the FAR clause set do not govern them.

options.text: Ensuring the recipient's technical performance meets the statement of work, and accepting or rejecting each deliverable for the Government as it arrives at the program office.
options.why: That is a procurement acceptance role; an assistance award supports a public purpose rather than delivering goods and services to the Government.

options.text: Ensuring funds are available for obligation, and leaving legal and policy compliance to the program office that requested the award.
options.why: Availability of funds is only one of the three; compliance with law, Executive orders, regulation and DoD policy is the grants officer's own responsibility.

cite: DoDGARs (32 CFR chapter I subchapter C); official CORB board answer Q0168

stem: How would you describe the purpose of the Other Transaction authorities?

options.text: Flexibility to use commercial business practices and reach state-of-the-art solutions from traditional and nontraditional firms through tailored teaming.
options.why: That is the stated purpose: flexibility to incorporate commercial standards and best practices, and access to current technology through tailored arrangements.

options.text: They let the Government buy commercial supplies and services faster by applying a much higher simplified acquisition threshold to research and prototype work.
options.why: OT authority is a different instrument, not a higher threshold inside the simplified acquisition rules.

options.text: They exist so the Government can award to nontraditional defense contractors without competing the requirement at all.
options.why: Broadening the industrial base is a benefit, but it is reached through competition to the maximum extent practicable, not by skipping competition.

options.text: They give the Government a way to fund university research in place of grants and cooperative agreements when the assistance paperwork is far too burdensome.
options.why: Assistance for a public purpose runs through grants and cooperative agreements; the OT is not a substitute assistance instrument.

cite: DoD Other Transactions Guide; official CORB board answer Q0176

stem: What business acumen does an agreements officer need to negotiate, award and administer Other Transactions?

options.text: Judgment in an unstructured setting: weigh every business option, Government and commercial, and negotiate terms that balance risk while protecting the Government's rights and the law.
options.why: The agreements officer is expected to exercise that level of responsibility and judgment and is ultimately responsible for the terms that allocate risk.

options.text: Command of the FAR clause matrix, so the mandatory clauses are carried correctly into each agreement.
options.why: OT terms are negotiated rather than prescribed, so there is no mandatory clause set to carry across.

options.text: A working library of previously issued OTs and approved models, so each new agreement follows one that already worked and passed legal and policy review.
options.why: The guidance says specifically not to merely copy prior agreements, templates or models but to consider all possible business options.

options.text: Enough technical depth to write the prototype's performance requirements without relying on the program office's engineers and testers.
options.why: The agreements officer's contribution is business judgment and risk allocation, not replacing the program office's technical work.

cite: DoD Other Transactions Guide; official CORB board answer Q0178

stem: What does the Government normally provide in a solicitation for a prototype Other Transaction?

options.text: A clear problem statement, area of need or capability gap, so industry can propose very different solutions.
options.why: The Government states the problem or gap and leaves trade space for a wide range of industry solutions.

options.text: A performance work statement with measurable standards and a quality assurance surveillance plan for the prototype.
options.why: That is the FAR services construct; a prototype OT solicitation states the problem and leaves the solution to industry.

options.text: Detailed design specifications, so the proposals that come back can be compared directly on price and schedule alone.
options.why: Design specifications close the innovative trade space the solicitation is meant to open, and proposals are expected to differ in approach, schedule and cost.

options.text: A Government estimate and a list of approved partners the awardee is required to team with throughout the project.
options.why: Teaming arrangements are proposed by industry and tailored to the project and participants, not dictated in the solicitation.

cite: DoD Other Transactions Guide; official CORB board answer Q0179

stem: Before staffing an Other Transaction determination and findings through ODASA(P), with whom does the agreements officer coordinate?

options.text: The program office or other requiring activity representatives, the SCO or HCA, and local legal counsel.
options.why: Those three coordinations happen before the D&F is staffed through ODASA(P).

options.text: The program office only; legal review follows after ODASA(P) returns the approved determination.
options.why: Local legal counsel is part of the coordination before staffing, not a step after approval.

options.text: The senior procurement executive directly, since the determination is prepared under 10 U.S.C. 4022.
options.why: Approval may run to that level, but the agreements officer coordinates locally first and staffs the document through ODASA(P).

options.text: The prospective OT recipient, so the findings match the terms the parties have already discussed.
options.why: The determination is the Government's own analysis; coordinating it with the recipient puts that analysis in the wrong hands.

cite: 10 U.S.C. 4022(a)(2)(A) and (8); official CORB board answer Q0180

stem: What risks must the agreements officer assess in the determination and findings supporting an OTA, and how are they stated?

options.text: Cost, technical and schedule risk, each rated low, moderate or high, with the action-specific risks, why they earn that level, and the planned mitigation.
options.why: The D&F addresses all three risk types with a stated level, action-specific findings and mitigation plans.

options.text: Cost, technical, schedule and past performance risk, each scored against the participant's CPARS record and its prior OT experience with the Army and the rest of DoD.
options.why: The determination covers cost, technical and schedule risk; CPARS is a FAR past-performance tool and is not the measure here.

options.text: One overall risk rating for the project, supported by the program office's independent cost and schedule estimate.
options.why: Each of the three risk types carries its own level and its own mitigation; a single rating does not meet the requirement.

options.text: Only the risks the Government bears, since the other party's risk is its own business under a negotiated agreement.
options.why: The risk inherent in the prototype project and the capability of the expected sources shape the terms, so the assessment is not limited that way.

cite: DoD Other Transactions Guide; official CORB board answer Q0182 (D&F in support of an OTA: cost, technical and schedule risk)

stem: A board member asks you to describe an Other Transaction. What is the correct description?

options.text: A flexible, legally binding instrument of three types: research (10 U.S.C. 4021), prototype (4022) and follow-on production (4022(f)).
options.why: Flexible, legally binding, and three types is exactly how the authority is organized.

options.text: A nonbinding agreement to collaborate on research that becomes binding only when a production contract or a follow-on order follows it.
options.why: An OT is legally binding from the start; follow-on production is a separate type, not what creates the obligation.

options.text: A flexible instrument with two types, research and prototype, with any production work always requiring a separate FAR-based production contract.
options.why: Follow-on production under 4022(f) is the third type of Other Transaction.

options.text: An assistance instrument used when the principal purpose is to support a public purpose rather than acquire.
options.why: That describes grants and cooperative agreements; an Other Transaction is neither.

stem: Under the Army's delegation of approval authority for Other Transactions, who approves an OT valued at $75 million?

options.text: The head of the contracting activity, who holds approval for actions greater than $50 million up to $100 million.
options.why: The $75 million action falls in the HCA's band, above the SCO's $50 million ceiling and below the $100 million line.

options.text: The senior contracting official, whose approval authority runs up to $50 million.
options.why: The SCO's delegation stops at $50 million, so it does not reach a $75 million action.

options.text: The senior procurement executive, ASA(ALT), who approves actions greater than $100 million up to $500 million.
options.why: The senior procurement executive's band begins above $100 million.

options.text: The Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment or for Research and Engineering.
options.why: That level is reserved for actions greater than $500 million.

cite: Official CORB board answer Q0184 (Army OT approval thresholds by dollar value; no regulatory cite in the source)

stem: A board asks how your experience, training and business acumen prepare you for the latitude a grants officer has. What standard is the board measuring you against?

options.text: The DoDGARs standard: the appointing official's judgment of your experience, training, education, acumen and knowledge, which also sets the work you are given.
options.why: DoDGARs 21.440 makes those attributes the selection standard and ties the level of work assigned to them.

options.text: A fixed number of courses and years served in a grants office, after which the appointment follows automatically.
options.why: The standard is the appointing official's judgment about the candidate's attributes, not a course count or time in the seat.

options.text: The same warrant criteria used for contracting officers, because a grants officer appointment is just a contracting officer warrant issued through VCE-Warrants.
options.why: Grants officer selection runs on the DoDGARs standard for assistance instruments, a separate appointment from a KO warrant, however it is recorded.

options.text: Whether you can recite the cost principles, since the allowability of recipient costs is what a grants officer decides.
options.why: Knowledge of assistance instruments is one attribute among several; the standard is broader than the cost principles.

cite: DoDGARs 21.440; Army Warranting Program v7 para 4.2

stem: A pricing report that includes the technical evaluation recommends a Government position on direct labor well below the proposed amount. What do you rely on in developing your objective, and what do you seek in negotiations?

options.text: Check the data behind the report and other sources such as BLS or Global Insight, and ask for the offeror's labor spreadsheet and cost narrative.
options.why: The objective rests on data you have examined, and the spreadsheet and cost narrative are what let the Government validate the labor figures.

options.text: Adopt the report's figure as the objective, since it is the Government's independent position and the offeror can rebut it at the negotiating table.
options.why: The data source behind the recommendation has to be considered first; an unexamined figure will not hold up in negotiations.

options.text: Require the offeror to submit certified cost or pricing data on direct labor before you open negotiations.
options.why: The gap is closed with the supporting spreadsheet, cost narrative and other labor data sources, not by demanding certified data the action may not require.

options.text: Set the objective midway between the proposed labor cost and the report's recommended figure, so that both of the positions are fairly represented in it.
options.why: An objective has to rest on analyzed data, not on a mechanical midpoint between two numbers.

stem: In a formal source selection, what is the contracting officer's role in relation to the SSEB, the source selection advisory council and the source selection authority?

options.text: The PCO is the main business advisor and guidance source for the source selection and the focal point for all contact with companies.
options.why: That is how the DoD source selection guidance frames the PCO's role, and it is why the PCO should have prior source selection experience.

options.text: The contracting officer chairs the evaluation board and consolidates the consensus ratings into one report for the source selection authority.
options.why: The contracting officer ensures the evaluation chair evaluates against the stated criteria; the KO's own role is business advisor and guidance source.

options.text: The contracting officer makes the selection decision whenever the advisory council and the evaluation board disagree on the final ranking.
options.why: The source selection decision belongs to the source selection authority; the contracting officer advises and documents.

options.text: The contracting officer stays out of all exchanges with offerors so that the evaluation team's independence is preserved until the award.
options.why: The opposite: the KO is the focal point for all communications with companies, conducts discussions and gives debriefings.

cite: DoD Source Selection Procedures; official CORB board answer Q0214

stem: GAO notifies your agency that a protest has been filed before you have made award, and the requiring activity presses you to award anyway. What allows award to proceed?

options.text: A written, nondelegable HCA finding that urgent and compelling circumstances will not permit waiting for GAO, with award likely within 30 days.
options.why: That is the only preaward exception; both elements must be met and the agency notifies GAO of the finding before award.

options.text: A written head of the contracting activity finding that proceeding with award is in the best interests of the Government, with notice sent to GAO.
options.why: Best interests is a postaward override ground, notice or not; before award the finding must be urgent and compelling circumstances plus award likely within 30 days.

options.text: The contracting officer's own determination, documented in the file, that the protest grounds have no merit.
options.why: The contracting officer cannot override the bar on award; the finding belongs to the head of the contracting activity and cannot be delegated.

options.text: Permission from GAO to proceed with award, which the agency requests when it files the agency report.
options.why: GAO does not authorize award; the agency proceeds on the HCA's finding and notifies GAO of it before award.

stem: A new LCS purchase request for grounds maintenance services arrives with an independent government estimate of $11 million. What does that dollar value mean for the way you run the procurement?

options.text: Simplified acquisition is not available at this value, so run a source selection with a plan, and build the approvals into the schedule; confirm the levels with C&P.
options.why: At $11 million simplified acquisition is off the table and a source selection plan is required, with the approval requirements for that dollar value built into the schedule.

options.text: Simplified acquisition procedures still apply, because grounds maintenance is a commercial service and the work is recurring each year.
options.why: Commercial or not, simplified procedures cannot be used at this dollar value.

options.text: No source selection plan is needed, because the field of eligible firms is small and the award decision will be price-driven.
options.why: A small field does not remove the source selection plan; an action of this size requires one.

options.text: Break the requirement into smaller annual actions so each one falls below the simplified acquisition threshold.
options.why: Dividing a requirement to avoid a threshold is improper; the approved requirement is an $11 million action.

cite: Official CORB board answer Q0276; USFK LCS Program under the Special Measures Agreement (confirm approval levels and current procedures with C&P)

stem: A contract specialist new to ABG-75 joins your team. How do you bring them up to speed and what tools do you put in their hands?

options.text: Teach the procedures with the ABG-75 guidance book and hands-on work, and send their questions to the IMCOM-E ABG-75 representative and the division chief.
options.why: The guidance book plus hands-on training is the tool set, and the IMCOM-E ABG-75 representative and the division chief are where the questions go.

options.text: Keep them on FAR-based actions for the first year, since ABG-75 work follows the same rules once the FAR is second nature and the ABG forms have been learned.
options.why: ABG-75 has its own procedures and its own guidance book; FAR fluency does not substitute for learning them.

options.text: Give them the regulation and guidance book to work through on their own, and check their progress with a short written quiz at the end of each training quarter.
options.why: The book alone is not the training; hands-on work and access to the ABG-75 representative are what build competence.

options.text: Enroll them in the DAU (WARU) contracting courses and hold their file assignments until the certificates are complete.
options.why: Those courses do not teach ABG-75; the procedures come from the guidance book, hands-on training and the IMCOM-E representative.

cite: ABG 75 procedures (Germany); official CORB board answer Q0279 (confirm current local procedures with the IMCOM-E ABG-75 representative)

stem: An ABG-75 contract requires a modification. Which change order documents are used, and who initiates each?

options.text: ABG5a: the Government tells the Bauamt of a requirement or administrative change. ABG5: the Bauamt sends changes with a justification, which DPW reviews.
options.why: Those are the two change order documents and the direction each one travels.

options.text: The ABG5, which the Government issues unilaterally, and the ABG5a, which the contractor submits as a claim for additional work.
options.why: It is the reverse: the Government initiates the ABG5a, and the ABG5 comes to us from the Bauamt with its justification.

options.text: An SF 30 for administrative changes such as a new line of accounting, and an ABG5 for any change in the requirement.
options.why: ABG-75 changes run on the ABG5a and ABG5 documents, and an administrative change such as a line of accounting is made by ABG5a.

options.text: Only the ABG5, which covers every kind of change, with an administrative change such as a new line of accounting needing no document at all, only a note in the file.
options.why: There are two documents, and an administrative change is documented by ABG5a rather than going unrecorded or into a note in the file.

cite: ABG 75 procedures (Germany); official CORB board answer Q0280 (ABG5 and ABG5a change order documents; confirm current local requirements with the 409th CSB)

stem: Why is it important to fully document the contract file?

options.text: For continuity, compliance, defending your decisions to the Army or German government, and protecting the Army in litigation.
options.why: Continuity, compliance, defensibility and litigation protection are the four reasons the file has to be complete.

options.text: So the file can be assembled and reviewed at closeout, which is the point when the complete record is first required by regulation.
options.why: The record is built as the action proceeds; a file assembled at closeout cannot tell a successor where the action stands today.

options.text: Because a complete file is what authorizes the contracting officer to take any further action on the contract with the Bauamt.
options.why: Authority comes from the warrant; the file records and defends the decisions that authority supports.

options.text: So that the contractor has a full record of the Government's internal deliberations if a dispute with the Bauamt arises later on.
options.why: The file exists to protect the Army's interests; it is not compiled for the contractor's benefit.

cite: ABG 75 procedures (Germany); official CORB board answer Q0281 (contract file documentation)

stem: USFK J4 sends you an approved LCS requirement to replace rooftop HVAC units on three barracks at Camp Humphreys, IGE $1.8 million. A U.S. HVAC company with a Pyeongtaek office asks to be added to the bidders list, and the DPW engineer would prefer it because it installed the original units. What do you do?

options.text: Tell the firm plainly that this LCS-funded action is limited to Korean firms by program rule, and keep its capability statement for O&M work.
options.why: LCS is ROK money under the Special Measures Agreement and the program is limited to Korean businesses, so the honest answer to the firm is that it cannot compete on this one.

options.text: Add the firm to the list, since excluding a capable local offeror without a written justification and approval would improperly restrict competition.
options.why: The Korean-firm limitation is a rule of the LCS program under the international agreement, not a restriction the contracting officer imposes or may waive.

options.text: Add the firm as a proposed subcontractor to the eventual Korean awardee so the original installer's knowledge is not lost.
options.why: The program expects Korean material and labor; routing the U.S. firm in through a side channel is not a call the KO makes on an MND-awarded action.

options.text: Tell the engineer you can limit the competition to that firm because it installed the original units and knows the system.
options.why: A limited-competition justification is a FAR tool for U.S. actions; it cannot override the LCS program limitation, and the competition here is already limited to Korean firms.

cite: U.S.-ROK Special Measures Agreement (LCS); RFO FAR 6.103-4 (international agreement); 411th CSB LCS SOP (confirm current documentation and publicizing procedure with C&P)

stem: Evaluation is complete on an LCS-funded purchase of twelve non-tactical vehicles, about $2.4 million, and the apparent successful offeror is a Korean dealer. The transportation officer asks you to sign the award tomorrow so the vehicles arrive before the first snow. What can you sign?

options.text: Only the recommendation for award, routed through J4; you prepare the contract for the USFK LCS program manager and ROK MND to approve and sign.
options.why: The funds are ROK funds held by MND, so the KO's product is a recommendation for award and MND approves and awards.

options.text: Sign the award now and route the package to J4 and MND afterward so they can ratify the action.
options.why: The KO has no award authority on an LCS action, so there is no Government award for MND to ratify.

options.text: Sign the award and record the obligation in the U.S. accounting system so the Korean dealer can invoice through WAWF like any other U.S. vendor would.
options.why: No U.S. funds are involved; invoices go to ROK MND and MND pays, so there is no U.S. obligation to record.

options.text: Tell the transportation officer to have the dealer start delivery on a verbal go-ahead while the whole package routes through J4 and MND for approval.
options.why: A vendor that starts on a verbal from the customer has no contract with anyone, which is the same unauthorized commitment problem as on the O&M side.

cite: U.S.-ROK Special Measures Agreement (LCS); RFO FAR 1.405 (unauthorized commitments); 411th CSB LCS SOP (confirm current procedure and invoice mechanics with C&P and J4)

stem: On an LCS package for dining facility refrigeration repair, the winning Korean offeror's replacement compressors are made in Japan; all other parts and all labor are Korean. The DPW engineer tells you to write "local materials" on the memo going to J4 because MND never checks. What do you do?

options.text: Write the memo truthfully: name the Japanese compressors as offshore, note the rest is Korean and your search for Korean alternatives, and ask J4 how MND treats offshore parts this year.
options.why: The memo is a written representation to J4 and to the government paying the bill, so it states the facts and gives MND what it needs to decide.

options.text: Write "local materials," since the labor and nearly all of the parts are Korean and the memo is only a summary characterization.
options.why: A knowingly false representation is an integrity problem whatever the size of the offshore portion, and whether MND checks is not the standard.

options.text: Reject the offer yourself as ineligible, since an offshore component does not meet the LCS expectation of Korean material and labor on every single part it supplies.
options.why: Whether an offshore component is acceptable inside an LCS award is an MND and LCS program decision, not one the contracting officer makes alone.

options.text: Leave the memo out of this package, because since January 2022 MND no longer requires an offshore waiver before submission.
options.why: The 2022 change removed the pre-approved waiver, not the requirement that a memo documenting offshore or local materials accompany every LCS package to J4.

cite: U.S.-ROK Special Measures Agreement (LCS); RFO FAR 1.402-2; DoD 5500.07-R (Joint Ethics Regulation); 411th CSB LCS SOP (offshore/local materials memo; confirm current format and MND practice with C&P)

stem: One week before releasing a $3.2 million LCS grounds maintenance solicitation, the DPW chief asks you to add about $400,000 of FY27 O&M-funded tree removal line items so there is one competition and one contractor. What do you tell him?

options.text: They cannot share one solicitation: O&M needs full and open competition and LCS is limited to Korean firms, and one document cannot carry both rules.
options.why: Combining them would either restrict the O&M work to Korean firms unlawfully or open LCS work to non-Korean firms against the program rule.

options.text: It can be done if the solicitation restricts only the LCS line items to Korean firms and leaves the O&M line items open to every interested U.S. and Korean firm.
options.why: Splitting the restriction inside one solicitation does not cure it; the O&M work would still be solicited under a document that limits the competition.

options.text: It can be done because the combined value stays within one competitive action and the resource manager has already certified the FY27 O&M funds in writing.
options.why: Certified funds and total value are not the obstacle; the competition rules and the separate award and payment paths are.

options.text: Add the line items and obligate the O&M funds at award, since MND will award the whole contract and the U.S. share is reimbursed to ROK MND afterward.
options.why: MND approves, awards and pays the LCS portion, while a U.S. O&M action carries the KO's own award signature and is paid through DFAS.

cite: RFO FAR 6.101; RFO FAR 6.103; RFO FAR 6.103-4; U.S.-ROK Special Measures Agreement (LCS); 411th CSB study material (O&M and LCS cannot be combined in one solicitation)

stem: An approved LCS requirement for custodial and grounds maintenance across Area III arrives with an IGE of $14 million, a base period plus four options. Your last three LCS actions were under $2 million using simplified procedures. What governs your approach at this value?

options.text: Part 15 negotiation: the commercial simplified ceiling is $9 million, and above $10 million DoD procedures require an SSA-approved source selection plan before release; confirm the SSA with C&P.
options.why: Neither the SAT nor the $9 million commercial ceiling reaches $14 million, and the DoD procedures above $10 million call for an SSA-approved plan before release.

options.text: Commercial simplified procedures, because custodial and grounds maintenance are commercial services and the competition is limited to Korean firms in any case, so the dollar value does not matter.
options.why: The commercial simplified procedures stop at $9 million, so at $14 million they are unavailable however commercial the services are or however the competition is limited.

options.text: Part 15 procedures, but no source selection plan is required, because MND rather than the Army makes the award decision on an LCS action.
options.why: The package is still built under U.S. procedures, and the source selection planning requirement attaches to how you run the competition.

options.text: Simplified procedures for the base period alone, with each option evaluated separately as MND approves it in its own program year.
options.why: The acquisition is valued at $14 million including options; the base period cannot be carved out to bring it under a threshold.

cite: RFO FAR 12.201-1; RFO FAR 2.101; RFO FAR 15.103; RFO DFARS 215.201(b)(2); DoD Source Selection Procedures (20 Aug 2022); 411th CSB LCS SOP (confirm SSA level and templates with C&P)

stem: On 14 September an Area I DPW sends you an LCS purchase request for snow and ice removal, 1 November through 31 March, asking you to award before 30 September "so we do not lose the FY26 money." What do you tell them?

options.text: There is no FY26 money to lose: LCS funds are ROK money held by MND, so the ROK program year and MND approval set the dates; confirm them with J4.
options.why: The U.S. fiscal year does not govern ROK funds; what governs is whether the requirement is on the approved program-year list and how long MND approval takes.

options.text: Award before 30 September, because the requirement was submitted in FY26 and the funds supporting it expire at the end of the U.S. fiscal year on 30 September.
options.why: LCS funds are not a U.S. appropriation, so U.S. fiscal-year expiration does not reach them.

options.text: Award before 30 September and rely on the 12-month severable services authority to carry the snow season's performance period into the next fiscal year.
options.why: That authority is a U.S. fiscal law tool for appropriated funds; it has nothing to do with ROK money held by MND.

options.text: Split the requirement into two actions before sending it to J4, because the period of performance crosses 31 December.
options.why: How MND treats a period that straddles its program years is a question for J4 and MND, not an assumption the contracting officer acts on.

cite: U.S.-ROK Special Measures Agreement (LCS); USFK Reg 37-5 (2007); 31 U.S.C. 1502; 10 U.S.C. 3133; 411th CSB LCS SOP (confirm the current program-year calendar with J4 and C&P)

stem: You are awarding a $4.6 million O&M contract for simulator maintenance at Osan, and the U.S. manufacturer will send six U.S. technicians to Korea for 18 months. The project officer asks whether SOFA status is the contractor's problem. What is your part before award?

options.text: You request the contract's SOFA designation from USFK/FKAQ under Article XV and USFKI 4901.01; the requiring activity requests the individuals'.
options.why: Invited contractor designation is a two-step process, and the contract-level request is the contracting officer's responsibility.

options.text: None of it: once it is on contract, the contractor applies to FKAQ for invited contractor status for itself and for each one of its six technicians.
options.why: The contract-level designation is requested by the contracting officer, and the individual designations come through the requiring activity as sponsor.

options.text: Both steps are yours: request the contract designation and the individual designations for all six technicians at the same time, well before award.
options.why: Designation of individual contractor employees belongs to the requiring activity, not the contracting officer.

options.text: Determine the technicians' SOFA status yourself and state it in the contract so the contractor can plan their travel, housing and installation access.
options.why: FKAQ determines status and notifies the contracting officer; a KO cannot confer it by writing it into the contract.

cite: U.S.-ROK SOFA Article XV; USFKI 4901.01 (USFK/FKAQ Invited Contractor and Technical Representative Program); RFO FAR 25.802; RFO DFARS 225.770(c) (confirm current FKAQ procedure with C&P)

stem: On a SOFA-designated services contract at Camp Humphreys, the U.S. contractor wants to hire a Korean national engineer locally and asks the COR whether she will receive SOFA status. What is the answer?

options.text: No. Article XV covers people ordinarily resident in the United States who are in Korea only to perform U.S. contracts; Korean hires fall under ROK labor law.
options.why: A Korean national hired in Korea is not ordinarily resident in the United States and does not become an invited contractor by working for one.

options.text: She receives status as soon as the contractor adds her to its employee roster, because the contract itself is already SOFA designated by FKAQ for all of its staff.
options.why: Designation attaches to the contract and to named individuals; it does not extend automatically to everyone the contractor hires.

options.text: The COR can approve it, since the COR administers daily performance and maintains the contractor's staffing roster.
