options.why: CORs make no SOFA determinations; individual requests go through the requiring activity and FKAQ decides.

options.text: She receives status if the contracting officer adds her name to the FKAQ request covering this contract.
options.why: No request by the contracting officer can make a locally hired Korean national ordinarily resident in the United States, which is what Article XV requires.

cite: U.S.-ROK SOFA Article XV; USFKI 4901.01; USFK SOFA contract clause (IC/TR status; Korean national labor under ROK labor law); confirm current FKAQ procedure with C&P

stem: Two Korean bus companies ask to price a Camp Humphreys shuttle service in won because all of their costs are in won, and the customer asks whether the Government or the contractor "eats the exchange rate." What governs the currency decision and its funding?

options.text: The contracting officer picks the currency before release; if it is won, the agency must hold enough funds to cover rate swings so no Anti-Deficiency Act violation occurs.
options.why: Currency is the KO's determination for performance outside the United States, and foreign-currency pricing carries an explicit funding obligation to cover fluctuation.

options.text: Offerors choose the currency they prefer, and the Government converts each offer at the exchange rate in effect on the date of award to compare them on a fully equal basis.
options.why: The KO decides, and where more than one currency is permitted the conversion uses the rate source and date named in the solicitation provision, not the award date.

options.text: Pricing must be in U.S. dollars on a U.S.-funded contract, so the contractor carries the exchange risk as a cost of doing business.
options.why: For performance outside the United States the contracting officer may require a specified foreign currency; dollar pricing is a choice, not a rule.

options.text: Pricing in won is permitted only if the contract carries an economic price adjustment clause tied to a published daily exchange rate index from the Bank of Korea.
options.why: A fixed-price contract with economic price adjustment is the alternative when dollar pricing is kept, not a condition on pricing in won, whatever index is used.

cite: RFO FAR 25.1002-1; RFO FAR 25.1002-2; FAR 52.225-17; 31 U.S.C. 1341; DoD FMR 7000.14-R Volume 5, Chapter 13; RFO FAR 16.203

stem: Your U.S. prime, designated for SOFA invited contractor status, will subcontract trenching and cabling to a Korean construction firm, and asks whether the subcontractor gets SOFA status and can invoice the prime without Korean value-added tax. What do you tell the prime?

options.text: The prime's status does not reach a Korean subcontractor, which needs no designation, and you promise no tax result; the SOFA exemption covers the Government's own buys, so refer tax questions to C&P's procedure.
options.why: Article XV reaches persons ordinarily resident in the United States, and the tax exemption belongs to the Government's contract, not to a private sale between the subcontractor and the prime.

options.text: The subcontractor takes the prime's invited contractor status for work under a SOFA-designated contract, so its invoices to the prime are tax exempt as well, with no VAT added.
options.why: Designation is made by FKAQ for the contract and for named individuals; it does not pass through to a Korean subcontractor, and no tax result follows from it.

options.text: You must request FKAQ designation for the Korean subcontractor before any of its crews may work on the installation.
options.why: A Korean firm needs no SOFA designation; getting its crews onto the installation is a garrison access control matter, not a SOFA question.

options.text: Since there is no privity with the subcontractor, you take no position and leave all three questions to the prime to resolve.
options.why: The prime is owed a written answer, and where the contract requires consent to subcontract the contracting officer has a decision to make.

cite: U.S.-ROK SOFA Article XV (invited contractors; tax exemption for official U.S. forces procurement); USFKI 4901.01; USFK SOFA contract clause (Korean national labor; FKAQ approval); RFO FAR 44.201-1; FAR 52.244-2 (confirm the current Korea tax exemption clause and procedure with C&P)

stem: An exercise support cell wants a $32,000 card buy and a $1.6 million tent-city life support award, citing overseas contingency thresholds of $40,000 and $2 million because its memo says USFK is "in a contingency posture." What actually governs?

options.text: Only a head-of-agency determination that the buy supports a contingency or listed event raises them. Without one in the file, $15,000 and $350,000 apply; ask C&P.
options.why: The higher overseas figures are conditional on that determination, and a scheduled exercise is not a contingency operation by itself.

options.text: They apply because both acquisitions are awarded and performed outside the United States, which is the only condition the FAR sets for the higher figures, with no other step needed.
options.why: Overseas performance is only half of the rule; the determination that the acquisition supports a contingency or similar event is what raises the thresholds.

options.text: They apply because the customer's memo states that USFK is in a contingency posture, which is the determination the FAR contemplates.
options.why: A customer memo is not a head-of-agency determination or a combatant commander authorization, and a posture is not a threshold.

options.text: They do not apply, so the $1.6 million life support package has to run as a Part 15 negotiated source selection.
options.why: Even at standard thresholds, commercial services may use simplified procedures well above this value, so a Part 15 source selection is not forced.

cite: RFO FAR 2.101; RFO FAR 18.001; 10 U.S.C. 101(a)(13); DoD Class Deviation 2024-O0011; RFO FAR 12.201-1 (confirm any exercise-specific authorization with the Chief, C&P)

stem: On a grounds maintenance and custodial services contract at Camp Walker staffed by about 40 Korean nationals, the requiring activity wants a Service Contract Labor Standards wage determination attached and an offeror asks whether it must pay the U.S. federal minimum wage. What is correct?

options.text: Neither applies: the statute covers only services in the United States, which excludes a U.S. base abroad, so Korean labor law governs under the local labor law clause.
options.why: Coverage turns on where the services are furnished, and a U.S. base within a foreign country is expressly outside the definition.

options.text: The wage determination applies, because work performed on a U.S. installation is treated as performance inside the United States for all labor standards purposes, even overseas.
options.why: A U.S. base within a foreign country is specifically excluded from the definition of the United States for this statute.

options.text: The wage determination does not apply, but the U.S. federal minimum wage still sets the floor for the contractor's employees on any U.S.-funded installation contract abroad.
options.why: The federal minimum wage is U.S. labor law with a U.S. geographic scope; it does not govern a Korean company's employees working in Korea.

options.text: Both apply, because the contract is funded with U.S. appropriations and is awarded and administered by a U.S. contracting officer under the FAR, the DFARS and other U.S. law.
options.why: Neither the funding source nor the identity of the awarding official extends the statute beyond services furnished in the United States.

cite: RFO FAR 22.001; RFO FAR Subpart 22.10; FAR 22.1001 (legacy definition of United States); 29 CFR 4.112; 41 U.S.C. chapter 67; RFO DFARS 222.7201(a); DFARS 252.222-7002

stem: An unsuccessful Korean offeror asks whether it can take your $2.4 million award to GAO, and a different Korean vendor asks about protesting to GAO an LCS award that ROK MND made on the 411th's recommendation. What is correct?

options.text: Yes for your award: interested party status rests on economic interest, not nationality. No for the LCS award: MND awarded and pays it, so the remedy runs through J4 to MND; confirm with legal.
options.why: A 411th award is a Federal procurement wherever it is performed, while the LCS award belongs to MND, which is not a Federal agency.

options.text: Neither may protest to GAO, because a foreign company is not an interested party under the GAO bid protest regulations.
options.why: Nationality is irrelevant: an interested party is an actual or prospective offeror whose direct economic interest would be affected by the award.

options.text: Both may protest to GAO, because the 411th ran the competition and made the award recommendation in each case.
options.why: Running the competition does not make the LCS action a Federal procurement; MND signs the contract and pays the invoices.

options.text: The unsuccessful offeror must exhaust the agency protest process before going to GAO, and the LCS vendor follows that same path through the 411th's agency protest first.
options.why: An agency protest is optional and does not extend the time for obtaining a stay at GAO, and the LCS vendor's remedy lies with MND, not with a 411th agency protest.

cite: 4 CFR 21.0; 4 CFR 21.1; 4 CFR 21.2; 31 U.S.C. 3551; RFO FAR 33.104-3; U.S.-ROK Special Measures Agreement (LCS; confirm current MND dispute procedures with USFK J4 and C&P)

stem: On an LCS-funded repair project that ROK MND awarded on the 411th's recommendation, the contractor is behind schedule and has pulled its crew to another job. The COR asks you to issue a cure notice and terminate for cause. What can you do?

options.text: Neither: MND holds the contract, so a 411th notice has no effect. Document the facts, recommend MND action to USFK J4 in writing, and confirm LCS procedures with C&P.
options.why: The funds are held and the contract signed by MND, so the remedy has to be driven through J4 to the party that holds privity.

options.text: Issue the cure notice under RFO FAR 49.607 and, if the response is inadequate, terminate for default and charge the excess reprocurement costs to the contractor under the Default clause.
options.why: Those are FAR remedies on a U.S. contract; this instrument was signed by MND, which holds privity with the contractor.

options.text: Direct the COR to issue the cure notice, since the COR observes performance every day and the 411th administers the project on the ground on behalf of USFK J4 and ROK MND.
options.why: CORs do not issue cure notices at all, and no one at the 411th can take a contractual remedy on MND's contract.

options.text: Terminate the work and reprocure it immediately as an O&M action so the roof is closed before the monsoon.
options.why: Replacement work stays LCS unless the customer re-funds it, and the two kinds of money cannot share a solicitation.

cite: U.S.-ROK Special Measures Agreement (LCS: MND holds the funds, USFK J4 manages, the KO recommends award, MND awards and pays); RFO FAR 49.607; RFO FAR 12.304 (the O&M contrast); current LCS procedures (confirm with USFK J4 and C&P)

stem: The garrison sends two O&M-funded purchase requests: $780,000 for Korean-made 45-passenger shuttle buses to replace a fleet permanently, and $420,000 for Korean-made pickup trucks. It asks whether the Berry Amendment or Buy American stops the purchases. What governs?

options.text: Neither: Berry does not list vehicles and Buy American covers use inside the U.S.; the Balance of Payments Program governs the trucks, and another statute requires buses made in the NTIB, which excludes Korea.
options.why: The customer named the wrong two rules; the real constraints are the Balance of Payments Program and the multipassenger vehicle restriction that blocks Korean-made buses.

options.text: Buy American applies to both, because these are U.S.-funded purchases made by a U.S. contracting officer, so each one needs a nonavailability determination before award.
options.why: Buy American is about supplies acquired for public use inside the United States, and its clause is not used for supplies for use outside it.

options.text: The SOFA permits local procurement without restriction as to choice of supplier, so both purchases may proceed as requested.
options.why: That freedom runs against Korean-imposed restrictions on whom the United States may deal with; it does not waive U.S. domestic source statutes.

options.text: The Berry Amendment blocks both, because it restricts end items procured for the use of the armed forces overseas.
options.why: Berry covers food, clothing and fabrics, tents, hand and measuring tools and flags; vehicles are not on its list.

cite: 10 U.S.C. 4862; DFARS 225.7002-1; RFO FAR 25.102; RFO FAR 25.601(a)(1)(i)(C); DFARS 225.7500 and 225.7501; 10 U.S.C. 4864; DFARS 225.7004-1 through 225.7004-3 (confirm current non-tactical vehicle policy with USFK J4 and C&P)

stem: Under RFO FAR 15.204-2, what must the contracting officer provide when negotiations with an offeror still in the competitive range are finished?

options.text: A chance to submit a written proposal revision, notice that award will follow without more revisions, and the same deadline as everyone else
options.why: RFO FAR 15.204-2(d) requires the written revision opportunity, the notice of intent to award without further revisions, and equal time for everyone still in the range.

options.text: A clarification request limited to minor or clerical errors, since under RFO FAR 15.202 clarifications are what formally close out negotiations
options.why: Clarifications under 15.202(a)(2) do not permit proposal revisions, so they cannot close out negotiations.

options.text: A final proposal revision under FAR 15.307(b), offered only to the offerors whose prices changed during negotiations with the Government
options.why: 15.307(b) is the pre-RFO number, and the revision opportunity goes to every offeror remaining in the competitive range, not just those whose prices changed.

options.text: Nothing further, because negotiating with the lowest-priced offeror alone satisfies the requirement
options.why: 15.204-2(b)(1) requires negotiations with each responsible offeror in the competitive range, at minimum on its deficiencies and significant weaknesses.

cite: RFO FAR 15.204-2(d)

stem: In a competitive cost-reimbursement source selection, how does RFO FAR 15.404-3 treat an offeror's unrealistically low proposed cost?

options.text: The Government adjusts cost elements to realistic levels to reach a probable cost, and uses that probable cost for best value
options.why: 15.404-3(b) requires a probable cost for each offeror on cost-reimbursement contracts and uses it to evaluate best value.

options.text: The proposed cost is evaluated as submitted, and realism affects only the technical risk rating assigned to the offeror's approach
options.why: That describes realism on competitive fixed-price contracts (15.404-3(c)), not cost-reimbursement awards.

options.text: The proposal is rejected as materially unbalanced under 15.404-6
options.why: Unbalanced pricing concerns line items that are over- or understated within a total price; it is not the realism test for cost-type contracts.

options.text: The offeror's fee is recomputed using the DFARS weighted guidelines profit objective
options.why: DFARS 215.404-970(b)(1) says not to perform a profit analysis when assessing cost realism in competitive acquisitions.

cite: RFO FAR 15.404-3(b)

stem: Which contractor argument is a valid defense to a Government price reduction for defective certified cost or pricing data?

options.text: The Government did not rely on the defective data
options.why: 10 U.S.C. 3706(b) makes non-reliance a valid defense, and RFO FAR 15.304(a)(2) requires the KO to consider the extent of reliance.

options.text: The contractor was the sole source, so the price would not have changed
options.why: 10 U.S.C. 3706(c)(1) and 15.304(a)(3)(i) say sole-source or superior bargaining position is not a defense.

options.text: The contracting officer should have known the data were defective
options.why: 10 U.S.C. 3706(c)(2) and 15.304(a)(3)(ii) expressly reject this defense.

options.text: The contractor never signed a Certificate of Current Cost or Pricing Data
options.why: Failing to submit a required certificate is not a defense (10 U.S.C. 3706(c)(4); 15.304(a)(3)(iv)).

stem: For negotiated DoD contracts with large businesses awarded on or after 1 October 2026, which one is exempt from CAS under 48 CFR 9903.201-1(b) as amended by the CAS Board final rule?

options.text: A $30 million cost-plus-fixed-fee contract with a large business
options.why: Amended 9903.201-1(b)(2) exempts negotiated contracts and subcontracts not in excess of $35 million.

options.text: A $40 million cost-plus-incentive-fee contract awarded after adequate price competition
options.why: The competition exemption at (b)(8) covers only firm-fixed-price contracts awarded without certified cost or pricing data, and $40 million exceeds the $35 million threshold.

options.text: A $36 million time-and-materials contract, because T&M is not a cost-reimbursement type
options.why: CAS applicability turns on the listed exemptions, not on contract type; a negotiated T&M contract over $35 million is not exempt.

options.text: A $120 million cost-plus-incentive-fee contract, because the business unit's prior-period CAS awards were under $100 million
options.why: $100 million is the full-versus-modified coverage threshold, not an exemption, and a single award of $100 million or more triggers full coverage.

stem: A DoD sole-source justification covers a $9.2 million base year and has a total value of $46 million with options. Who approves it?

options.text: The competition advocate, without power of delegation, because the total with options is $46 million
options.why: DFARS 206.104-71 Table 206-1 assigns justifications over $10 million and up to $100 million, options included, to the competition advocate, not delegable.

options.text: The contracting officer, by certification, because the base year is $10 million or less
options.why: RFO FAR 6.104-2(c) requires the value of all options in the approval tier, so the justification is valued at $46 million.

options.text: The head of the procuring activity, under the FAR Table 6-1 tier of over $20 million to $150 million for DoD
options.why: DoD uses DFARS Table 206-1 in lieu of FAR Table 6-1, and the HCA tier starts above $100 million.

options.text: The competition advocate, who may delegate approval to the chief of the contracting office
options.why: Table 206-1 marks the competition advocate tier as not delegable.

cite: DFARS 206.104-71 Table 206-1

stem: Under DFARS 216.507-5(c) and clause 252.216-7010, which DoD task order requires a postaward debriefing on request?

options.text: A $22 million order, when the request is received within 3 days of notification of the order award
options.why: DoD requires a debriefing for orders valued at $15 million or more, and the clause treats a request within 3 days of award notification as timely.

options.text: Only an order over $35 million, the DoD order protest floor
options.why: $35 million is the GAO jurisdiction floor for order protests (10 U.S.C. 3406(f)), not the debriefing threshold.

options.text: Only an order over $7.5 million, and only if the ordering KO chooses, under FAR 16.505
options.why: 16.505 is the pre-RFO number, and debriefings are required, not discretionary: Part 15 debriefings above $7.5 million (16.507-5(c)) and DoD's $15 million requirement.

options.text: Only an order over $10 million, the protest floor for orders
options.why: $10 million is the civilian-agency order protest floor (41 U.S.C. 4106(f)), not a DoD debriefing threshold.

stem: A DoD consolidation valued at $84 million including options shows $4.6 million in quantified benefits. Under RFO FAR 7.107-2(c)(3), are the benefits 'substantial'?

options.text: No. At $94 million or less, benefits must reach 10 percent of the estimated value, here $8.4 million
options.why: 7.107-2(c)(3)(i) sets the 10 percent test for values of $94 million or less.

options.text: Yes. Any quantified savings above the $2 million consolidation threshold count as substantial benefits
options.why: $2 million is only the trigger for a written determination (7.107-1(b)(1)), not the benefit test.

options.text: Yes. Reduced administrative and personnel costs always count as substantial benefits
options.why: 7.107-2(d) says reductions in administrative or personnel costs alone are not enough unless the savings are substantial.

options.text: The test does not apply, because DoD's $8 million substantial bundling threshold replaces it for DoD
options.why: The substantial bundling threshold adds documentation (7.107-2(c)(6)); it does not replace the benefit test.

stem: Using the AFARS Appendix GG delegations for services acquisition strategy review (Rev. 30), who approves the strategy for a $64 million services acquisition?

options.text: The HCA, delegable no lower than the chief of the contracting office (Category IV: $10 million to under $100 million)
options.why: Appendix GG Rev. 30 places Category IV with the HCA, delegable no lower than the CoCO.

options.text: DASA(P) or the Senior Services Manager, because every services strategy above $10 million goes to HQDA for review and approval
options.why: Only Categories I and II, which start at $250 million, go to the Army Acquisition Executive, delegable to DASA(P) or the SSM.

options.text: The SCO, the lowest level allowed for Category III
options.why: Category III covers $100 million to under $250 million; a $64 million requirement is Category IV.

options.text: No review is required, because legacy AFARS 5137.590 reviews start at $100 million
options.why: 5137.590 is the pre-RFO number, and Appendix GG sets review categories down to the SAT.

cite: AFARS 5137.890-2 and Appendix GG

stem: Under RFO FAR 19.109, which proposed award to a large business requires a small business subcontracting plan?

options.text: A $38 million negotiated contract performed in the United States with subcontracting possibilities
options.why: It exceeds $900,000, has subcontracting possibilities and fits no exemption; contract type and competition do not matter.

options.text: A $12 million services contract with subcontracting possibilities, performed entirely at Camp Humphreys, Korea
options.why: 19.109(b)(3) exempts contracts performed entirely outside the United States and its outlying areas.

options.text: A $1.8 million construction contract with subcontracting possibilities for a public facility in the United States
options.why: The construction threshold is $2 million, so $1.8 million does not require a plan.

options.text: A $750,000 negotiated supply contract performed in the United States with subcontracting possibilities
options.why: $750,000 was the threshold before the 1 October 2025 inflation adjustment (FAR Case 2024-001); a $750,000 contract does not exceed today's $900,000 threshold.

cite: RFO FAR 19.109(a)-(b)

stem: A large business on a DoD firm-fixed-price contract asks for progress payments at 90 percent of incurred costs. Under DFARS 232.501-1 and PGI 232.501-2, what is correct?

options.text: It exceeds DoD's 80 percent customary rate for large businesses, so it is unusual and needs advance DPCAP approval
options.why: DFARS 232.501-1(a) sets 80 percent for large and 90 percent for small businesses, and PGI 232.501-2 requires advance DPCAP approval for unusual arrangements.

options.text: 90 percent is DoD's customary rate for all contractors
options.why: 90 percent is DoD's customary rate only for small business concerns.

options.text: The KO may approve 90 percent if the contract also includes performance-based payments on some line items
options.why: The two methods cannot be combined on one contract (32.113(d); 32.1003(d)), even on different line items, and combining them would not make the rate customary.

options.text: 85 percent is DoD's customary rate for large businesses, so the KO may simply counteroffer 85 percent without further approval
options.why: 85 percent is the FAR's small business rate (32.501-1(a)); DoD's large-business rate is 80 percent.

cite: DFARS 232.501-1(a); DFARS PGI 232.501-2

stem: A DoD UCA has a $48 million not-to-exceed price. The contractor submitted a qualifying proposal before 50 percent of the NTE was obligated. What is the most that may be obligated before definitization?

options.text: 75 percent of the NTE, $36 million, and only as much as the undefinitized period requires
options.why: DFARS 217.7404-4(a) and 10 U.S.C. 3372(a)(2)(B) raise the limit to 75 percent after a timely qualifying proposal; 217.7404-4(b) limits obligations to actual needs.

options.text: 50 percent of the NTE, $24 million, regardless of the proposal
options.why: 50 percent is the limit before a qualifying proposal; a timely qualifying proposal allows up to 75 percent.

options.text: 80 percent of the NTE, the progress payment limit for undefinitized actions
options.why: 80 percent (32.501-1(d)) caps progress payments on undefinitized work; it is not the obligation limit.

options.text: 100 percent, if the funds expire at the end of the fiscal year
options.why: There is no fiscal-year-end exception to the obligation limits; waivers are for specific operational needs such as contingency, humanitarian or peacekeeping operations (217.7404-5(b)).

stem: After a timely GAO protest of a DoD contract award, who may authorize the awardee to continue performance, and on what basis?

options.text: The HCA, nondelegably, on a written best-interests or urgent-and-compelling finding, after notifying GAO
options.why: RFO FAR 33.105-3(b)(2)-(c) and 31 U.S.C. 3553(d)(3)(C) and (e) set the official, both bases and the notice requirement.

options.text: The garrison commander, as head of the requiring activity, on a written finding of mission necessity
options.why: Only the head of the contracting activity may authorize performance, and the authority cannot be delegated.

options.text: The contracting officer, once the agency report has been filed with GAO and legal counsel concurs in writing
options.why: The KO has no override authority; filing the agency report or getting counsel's concurrence does not lift the stay.

options.text: The HCA, on a best-interests finding, both before and after award
options.why: Best interests is available only after award; a preaward override requires urgent and compelling circumstances and award likely within 30 days (33.105-2(b)).

stem: A contractor submits a $4.3 million claim whose certification omits required language. Under RFO FAR 33.205-6(e), what relieves the contracting officer of the obligation to issue a final decision?

options.text: Notifying the contractor in writing, within 60 days of receiving the claim, of the reasons the certification is defective
options.why: 33.205-6(e) removes the obligation to decide only when that written notice goes out within 60 days.

options.text: Nothing needs to be done, because a defective certification means no claim exists and no clock starts
options.why: A defective certification is not the same as no certification: jurisdiction survives (33.205-2(c)), interest runs from receipt (33.205-3(c)), and the 60-day notice is required.

options.text: Returning the claim after the 90-day board appeal period has passed
options.why: The 90-day period is the contractor's time to appeal a final decision; it does not govern a defective certification.

options.text: Waiting for the DCAA audit, because the 60-day clock under FAR 33.211(c) starts when the audit is complete
options.why: 33.211 is the pre-RFO number, and the 60-day period runs from receipt of the claim, not from an audit.

cite: RFO FAR 33.205-6(e)

stem: A DoD firm-fixed-price contract awarded in 2024 is partially terminated for convenience in August 2026. When does the settlement require certified cost or pricing data and a mandatory audit referral?

options.text: When the settlement plus the estimate to complete the rest exceeds $2.5 million (the threshold for DoD primes awarded by 30 June 2026), and proposals at or above it go to audit
options.why: 15.403-3(b)(3)(ii)(B) treats settlements as modifications, DFARS 215.403-3(a) applies the prime contract's $2.5 million criteria, and 49.107(a) makes audit referral mandatory at the threshold.

options.text: Only above $10 million, because the settlement is negotiated after 30 June 2026
options.why: DFARS 215.403-3(a)(1) applies the same criteria as the prime contract being modified, and this prime was awarded before 1 July 2026.

options.text: Never, because termination settlements are not new contract awards, so they are exempt from certified cost or pricing data and from any mandatory audit referral under Part 49
options.why: 15.403-3(b)(3)(ii) expressly treats termination settlements as modifications that can require certified data, and 49.107(a) makes audit referral mandatory at the threshold.

options.text: Only if the TCO chooses, because audit referral under 49.107 is discretionary
options.why: 49.107(a) requires referral when the proposal meets or exceeds the certified cost or pricing data threshold; only proposals below it are discretionary.

stem: For a $14.6 million firm-fixed-price construction contract in the United States, what does RFO FAR Part 28 require?

options.text: A bid guarantee of 20 percent of the bid (capped at $3 million) and 100 percent performance and payment bonds unless less is justified
options.why: 28.101-1(a), 28.101-2(b), 28.102-1(a) and 28.102-2(b) set these requirements for construction over $150,000.

options.text: A performance bond only, because the payment bond requirement applies only to construction projects of $35 million or more in the United States
options.why: $35 million is the project labor agreement threshold (36.002(a)); payment bonds are required above $150,000.

options.text: Two alternative payment protections chosen by the KO instead of a payment bond
options.why: Alternative payment protections apply to construction over $35,000 but not over $150,000 (28.102-1(b)); above $150,000 the payment bond is required.

options.text: No bid guarantee, because the chief of the contracting office waiver in 28.101-1(c) covers all construction, with performance and payment bonds only
options.why: The waiver is a case-by-case determination for situations such as overseas construction, emergencies or sole-source awards, so the bid guarantee is still required here.

stem: Under the Brooks Act as implemented in RFO FAR 36.202, how is an architect-engineer contractor selected?

options.text: Rank at least three firms on published qualifications without price, then negotiate with the top firm, moving down only if talks fail
options.why: 36.202-1 through 36.202-3 and 40 U.S.C. 1103-1104 require qualifications-based ranking followed by sequential negotiation.

options.text: Use a best-value tradeoff under 15.103-1, with price at least as important as qualifications, and negotiate with the two highest-rated firms
options.why: A-E services use the Brooks Act procedures in Part 36, not Part 15 tradeoffs, and negotiation is with one firm at a time.

options.text: Award on lowest price technically acceptable among firms whose SF 330s are acceptable
options.why: Price is not a selection factor under the Brooks Act; it is negotiated after selection.

options.text: Negotiate with the top three firms at the same time and award to the lowest price
options.why: Negotiation is sequential, starting with the most highly qualified firm (36.202-3(a)-(b)).

cite: RFO FAR 36.202-1 through 36.202-3

stem: Under AFARS 5115.408-190, what must an Army contracting officer obtain before negotiating a pricing action?

options.text: Written approval of the prenegotiation objectives
options.why: AFARS 5115.408-190 requires written approval of the prenegotiation objectives before negotiation of any pricing action.

options.text: DCAA's written concurrence with the Government negotiation objective
options.why: Audit recommendations are advisory; the KO decides and explains in the PNM when they are not adopted (15.407(a)).

options.text: The contractor's Certificate of Current Cost or Pricing Data, dated the day the proposal was submitted
options.why: The certificate is executed at price agreement, dated as close as practicable to that date (15.403-4).

options.text: HCA approval of the price negotiation memorandum under FAR 15.406-3
options.why: 15.406-3 is the pre-RFO number, and neither the FAR nor AFARS 5115.408 makes the HCA the PNM approver.

stem: For a DoD task order valued above $7.5 million under a multiple-award contract, what must the fair notice include under RFO FAR 16.507-5(a)?

options.text: Clear requirements, a reasonable response time, and the significant factors and subfactors, including cost or price, with their relative importance
options.why: 16.507-5(a) lists exactly these three elements for orders above $7.5 million.

options.text: A competitive range determination and a written evaluation plan under 15.204-1
options.why: 16.507-2(a)(3) says orders are not subject to subpart 15.3 policies and no evaluation plan or competitive range is required.

options.text: Nothing formal; the KO may place the order using information already available on each awardee, such as its past orders and published catalog prices
options.why: That streamlined approach is allowed only for orders above the micro-purchase threshold but not above the SAT (16.507-3), whatever information is on hand.

options.text: A 30-day SAM.gov synopsis and a Part 6 justification and approval
options.why: Orders under multiple-award contracts are exempt from Part 6 competition requirements; justifications are needed only for exceptions to fair opportunity.

cite: RFO FAR 16.507-5(a)

stem: Under Department of Labor DBA Waiver No. 2026-02 for the Republic of Korea, which employee on a U.S. Army services contract at Camp Humphreys still requires DBA coverage?

options.text: A U.S. citizen hired in Texas to work at Camp Humphreys
options.why: The waiver does not apply to U.S. citizens, lawful U.S. residents or anyone hired in the United States.

options.text: A Korean national hired in Pyeongtaek who is covered by Korea's compulsory workers' compensation law, with an employer in full compliance
options.why: That is exactly the classification the waiver covers.

options.text: Every employee, because the contracting officer did not sign a waiver for this contract
options.why: Only the Secretary of Labor waives DBA (42 U.S.C. 1651(e)), and Waiver 2026-02 already applies to all U.S. agencies and contracts in Korea.

options.text: No employee, because DBA does not apply to services contracts
options.why: Public work includes projects or operations under service contracts connected with the national defense (42 U.S.C. 1651(b)(1); FAR 28.305(a)).

cite: DoL DBA Waiver No. 2026-02; 42 U.S.C. 1651(e)

stem: Under RFO FAR 42.1103, how long does a contractor have to comment on a CPARS evaluation, and who reviews a disagreement?

options.text: Up to 14 calendar days after notice; a level above the contracting officer reviews any disagreement
options.why: 42.1103(d)(2)-(3) and (e)(3) set the 14-day comment period and review above the KO.

options.text: 30 calendar days, and the contractor's rebuttal replaces the Government's rating once the assessor agrees
options.why: The period is 14 calendar days, and the evaluation remains an agency decision (42.1103(d)(3)); the contractor's comments join the record, they do not replace the rating.

options.text: 14 days, and the contracting officer's representative decides any disagreement after meeting the contractor
options.why: Disagreements are reviewed at a level above the contracting officer, not by the COR, meeting or not.

options.text: There is no comment period for final evaluations under FAR 42.1503
options.why: 42.1503 is the pre-RFO number, and contractors may comment on every evaluation.

cite: RFO FAR 42.1103(d)-(e)

stem: In a DoD source selection valued at $420 million, which body gives the SSA a written comparative analysis of proposals and an award recommendation?

options.text: The Source Selection Evaluation Board (SSEB)
options.why: The SSEB evaluates each proposal against the RFP factors but does not compare proposals or recommend an awardee unless the SSA asks.

options.text: The Source Selection Advisory Council (SSAC), including any minority opinions
options.why: The SSP makes the SSAC's primary role a written comparative analysis and recommendation, and an SSAC is required at $100 million or more unless waived.

options.text: The PCO, because FAR 15.201(a) makes the contracting officer the SSA by default
options.why: The DoD SSP requires an SSA other than the PCO at $100 million or more, and the PCO is not the comparative-analysis body.

options.text: Legal counsel, as part of its legal sufficiency review
options.why: Counsel reviews for legal sufficiency and advises the team; it does not rank proposals or recommend an awardee.

cite: DoD Source Selection Procedures (20 Aug 2022) para 1.4.3

stem: A competitive DoD acquisition has a $98 million base period and $27 million in options. Under the DoD Source Selection Procedures, which statement is correct?

options.text: Options count: at $125 million the agency head appoints an SSA other than the PCO, and an SSAC is required unless waived
options.why: The SSP's $100 million trigger expressly includes options and planned orders.

options.text: Only the base period counts, so the PCO may act as SSA and no SSAC is needed until the first option is actually exercised
options.why: This is the common misread; the SSP threshold includes options and planned orders from the start.

options.text: The PCO may waive the SSAC when the schedule is critical, by signing a memorandum for record that explains the schedule urgency
options.why: SSP waivers below $1 billion are approved by the senior procurement executive, not the PCO.

options.text: The HCA must personally serve as SSA for any source selection over $100 million, including all options and planned orders
options.why: The SSP requires an agency-head appointment of someone other than the PCO; it does not require the HCA to be the SSA.

cite: DoD Source Selection Procedures (20 Aug 2022) paras 1.2.3, 1.4.1.1, 1.4.3.1.2

stem: The SSA disagrees with the SSAC and selects a lower-priced, lower-rated proposal. Which statement about the SSDD is correct?

options.text: The SSA cannot depart from the SSAC recommendation without a waiver from the senior procurement executive, obtained before signing
options.why: The SSA is not bound by the SSAC recommendation when there is a rational basis for disagreeing; no such waiver exists, before or after signing.

options.text: Citing the Outstanding and Good adjectival ratings is sufficient support
options.why: The SSP says the SSA must not rely on adjectival ratings alone and must analyze the differences between proposals.

options.text: An SSDD is required only when award goes to a higher-priced offeror
options.why: The SSP requires an SSDD for every source selection, and declining a premium needs an explicit justification.

options.text: It must show the SSA's own comparative assessment and why the price premium was not worth paying, without having to quantify it
options.why: FAR 15.205 and SSP 3.9.3 require documented rationale for tradeoffs, including benefits associated with additional costs, without requiring quantification.

stem: Under RFO FAR 15.205 and the DoD Source Selection Procedures, how must an SSA document a tradeoff that pays a price premium?

options.text: Assign a dollar value to each strength so the premium can be compared arithmetically
options.why: Quantification is not required; a reasoned narrative tied to the RFP factors is what the rule demands.

options.text: Adopt the SSEB's adjectival ratings by reference in the SSDD, since the higher rating justifies the higher price
options.why: The SSP says the SSA must not rely on adjectival ratings alone and must analyze the differences between proposals.

options.text: Explain what the extra cost buys and why it is worth it; the tradeoff need not be quantified in dollars
options.why: FAR 15.205 requires rationale including benefits associated with additional costs and states the documentation need not quantify the tradeoffs.

options.text: Document it only when the SSA disagrees with the SSAC; otherwise the SSAC report serves as the decision record
options.why: An SSDD reflecting the SSA's independent judgment is required for every source selection, including when the SSA agrees with the SSAC.

stem: For an Army sole-source J&A valued at $340 million including options, who is the approval authority?

options.text: The senior procurement executive, because FAR Table 6-1 sends DoD actions over $150 million to the SPE
options.why: DoD applies Table 206-1 in lieu of Table 6-1; the DoD SPE tier begins above $500 million.

options.text: The HCA, delegable only to a general or flag officer or civilian equivalent (DFARS Table 206-1)
options.why: Table 206-1 places actions over $100 million up to $500 million with the HCA, and 206.104-71(a) limits delegation.

options.text: The competition advocate, without power of delegation
options.why: The competition advocate tier covers actions over $10 million up to $100 million.

options.text: The contracting officer's certification under FAR 6.104-1(a)(12)
options.why: Certification serves as the approval only at $10 million or below.

stem: Before award, an Army sole-source action grows from $480 million to $560 million including options. Which statement about the J&A is correct?

options.text: It must be amended and approved by the ASA(ALT) as senior procurement executive, who cannot delegate that approval
options.why: Table 206-1 puts actions over $500 million with the SPE, and 10 U.S.C. 3204(e)(1)(B)(iii) says the SPE approves without further delegation.

options.text: The HCA's earlier approval still covers the award because the J&A was approved before the options were added
options.why: AFARS 5106.104-90 requires an amended J&A when value grows beyond the prior approver's authority before award.

options.text: The ASA(ALT) may delegate the approval to the HCA because Table 206-1 marks the SPE tier delegable
options.why: The delegation in 206.104-71(b) applies only when the USD(A&S) is acting as the DoD SPE.

options.text: The competition advocate may approve the amendment because only the options changed
options.why: The approval level follows total value including options, and the competition advocate tier ends at $100 million.

stem: What is the certified cost or pricing data threshold for an Army prime contract awarded in October 2026?

options.text: $2.5 million
options.why: That is the governmentwide figure in RFO FAR 15.403-3(a); DoD uses it only for prime contracts awarded on or before June 30, 2026.

options.text: $35 million
options.why: $35 million is the CAS contract-level applicability threshold in 41 U.S.C. 1502(b)(1)(B), not the certified cost or pricing data threshold.

options.text: Any sole-source award above the simplified acquisition threshold
options.why: Sole source alone does not trigger certified data; the requirement applies above the dollar threshold unless an exception applies.

options.text: $10 million
options.why: 10 U.S.C. 3702(a)(1)(A) and DFARS 215.403-3(a) set $10 million for DoD prime contracts awarded after June 30, 2026.

stem: An Army contracting activity wants to waive certified cost or pricing data on a $260 million sole-source award. Who may grant the waiver, and what coordination is required?

options.text: The senior contracting official, under a written delegation from the HCA for waivers of this size
options.why: The exceptional-case waiver cannot be delegated, in writing or otherwise; SCO-level delegation exists only for the separate nontraditional defense contractor waiver in PGI 215.403-71(b)(5).

options.text: The contracting officer, with legal review, once price analysis shows the price is reasonable
options.why: A reasonable price is one required finding, but the contracting officer has no authority to waive the requirement.

options.text: The HCA, without delegation, after coordinating with the senior procurement executive
options.why: FAR 15.403-2(c)(4) and DFARS 215.403-71(b)(1) give the waiver to the HCA without delegation, and PGI 215.403-71(b)(1)(ii) requires SPE coordination above $100 million; for the Army, AFARS Appendix GG routes that coordination to the DASA(P).

options.text: The senior procurement executive must personally grant every waiver over $100 million, after HCA review
options.why: The HCA grants the waiver; above $100 million the SPE is coordinated with, not the approving official.

stem: A business unit with only DoD contracts is selected for a single $140 million CAS-covered award in November 2026; it had $60 million in net CAS-covered awards last period. What applies?

options.text: Modified coverage, because the unit's prior-period awards were under $100 million
options.why: The single-award test and the prior-period test are alternatives; the $140 million award alone triggers full coverage.

options.text: Full coverage, with a Disclosure Statement found adequate by the CFAO before award, unless the agency head authorizes otherwise
options.why: A single award of $100 million or more triggers full coverage and the pre-award Disclosure Statement requirement under DFARS 230.201-70(a)(1), 48 CFR 9903.202-1(b)(1) and FAR 30.301.

options.text: Full coverage, but the Disclosure Statement may be filed within 90 days after award, once the contract is signed
options.why: The 90-day grace in 9903.202-1(b)(2) belongs to the prior-period awards trigger (a business unit or segment test from 1 October 2026), not to a business unit selected for a $100 million award.

options.text: No CAS, because cost-type development contracts are exempt
options.why: Contract type does not exempt a negotiated contract above $35 million; the listed exemptions include small business and sealed bid awards.

stem: A DoD-only business unit with $40 million in prior-period net CAS-covered awards elects modified coverage on a $70 million negotiated cost-type award in December 2026. Which clause set is correct?

options.text: FAR 52.230-3 with DFARS 252.230-7996, Alternate A, plus FAR 52.230-6 with 252.230-7998, Alternate A
options.why: DFARS 230.205-70(b) prescribes 52.230-3 with Alternate A when the amount is at or above the 230.201-70(b) threshold and below $100 million and the offeror elects modified coverage.

options.text: FAR 52.230-2 with 252.230-7995, Alternate A, because the award exceeds $50 million
options.why: For DoD-only business units, full coverage starts at $100 million under DFARS 230.201-70(a)(1); $50 million is the superseded figure.

options.text: No CAS clauses, because the contract is below $100 million
options.why: $100 million is the full-coverage threshold, not the applicability threshold; contracts above $35 million are CAS-covered unless exempt.

options.text: FAR 52.230-3 alone, applying the $2.5 million to $50 million band printed in RFO FAR 30.205(b)(1)
options.why: For DoD-only business units the deviation's thresholds and the Alternate A clauses apply; the FAR Part 30 figures are out of date.

stem: Under the DFARS RFO class deviation, what earned value requirement applies to a $180 million cost-plus-incentive-fee development contract?

options.text: An EIA-748 compliant EVMS, with no formal compliance determination by the cognizant Federal agency
options.why: That describes the $50 million to under $100 million tier in DFARS 234.201-70(a)(1).

options.text: A validated EVMS, because the requirement starts at $50 million under DFARS 234.201
options.why: Those are the codified figures; the class deviation raised the tiers to $50 million and $100 million.

options.text: EVM is optional, a risk-based decision documented with a cost-benefit analysis
options.why: Optional, risk-based EVM applies only to cost or incentive contracts under $50 million.

options.text: An EVMS that the cognizant Federal agency has determined complies with EIA-748
options.why: DFARS 234.201-70(a)(2) applies that requirement to cost or incentive contracts of $100 million or more.

stem: A program manager wants the EVMS clause on a $300 million firm-fixed-price production contract. What does the DFARS RFO class deviation require?

options.text: EVM is mandatory at $100 million or more regardless of contract type
options.why: The $50 million and $100 million tiers apply to cost or incentive contracts, not firm-fixed-price contracts.

options.text: The contracting officer may add clause 252.234-7999 on their own judgment after documenting the decision and the program manager's written request in the contract file
options.why: For firm-fixed-price contracts the deviation requires a waiver obtained by the program manager, not a KO documentation decision, whatever the file shows.

options.text: It is discouraged on firm-fixed-price work; the program manager needs a waiver from the Milestone Decision Authority, backed by a business case analysis
options.why: DFARS 234.201-70(a)(4) and PGI 234.201-70(a)(4) set the waiver path for firm-fixed-price contracts.

options.text: The HCA must waive the exemption in writing, delegable to the chief of the contracting office
options.why: That HCA waiver covers the nontraditional defense contractor exemption, not EVM on firm-fixed-price contracts.

stem: An Army contracting activity plans a competitive single-award IDIQ with a $450 million ceiling including options and no J&A. Under DFARS 216.504-3(a)(4), who holds the determination authority, and what standard applies to the 'integrally related' basis?

options.text: The HCA in its own right, without any delegation; the orders must be so integrally related that only a single source can reasonably perform the work
options.why: The DFARS vests the authority in the SPE (an Army HCA acts only by delegation under AFARS Appendix GG), and the DoD standard is 'efficiently,' not the FAR's 'reasonably.'

options.text: The SPE (for the Army, delegated to the HCA and redelegable no lower than the SCO); the orders must be so integrally related that only one source can efficiently do the work
options.why: DFARS 216.504-3(a)(4)(i) gives the determination to the SPE and substitutes 'efficiently perform' under 10 U.S.C. 3403(d)(3); Appendix GG Rev 30 delegates the Army authority to the HCA, redelegable no lower than the SCO.

options.text: The contracting officer, by documenting in the acquisition plan why multiple awards are not in the Government's interest
options.why: KO documentation under 16.504-3(a)(2) is required for every IDIQ, but above $150 million a head-of-agency determination is also required.

options.text: The head of the agency, who must also notify Congress within 30 days of any determination
options.why: The 30-day notice applies only to the public-interest basis, and DFARS 216.504-3(a)(4)(ii) says it does not apply to DoD.

stem: Under RFO FAR 16.504-3(a)(4), above what estimated value does a single-award task or delivery order contract require a written head-of-agency determination?

options.text: $150 million, including all options
options.why: RFO FAR 16.504-3(a)(4)(i) sets the threshold at $150 million including all options, applied in DoD through DFARS 216.504-3(a)(4).

options.text: $150 million, counting only the base ordering period
options.why: The threshold expressly includes all options.

options.text: $100 million, including all options
options.why: 10 U.S.C. 3403(d)(3) prints $100 million, but the FAR applies the inflation-adjusted figure of $150 million.

options.text: $7.5 million, the enhanced fair opportunity tier
options.why: $7.5 million is the fair opportunity ordering tier in FAR 16.507-5, not the single-award contract threshold.

stem: A DoD multiyear supply contract will include a $260 million cancellation ceiling. What does RFO FAR 17.104-3 require before award?

options.text: Written notice to the appropriations committees only, because the ceiling exceeds $20 million, with award after 31 days
options.why: The $20 million notice rule in 17.104-3(a) applies only to agencies other than DoD, NASA and the Coast Guard; for DoD the trigger is over $200 million and notice goes to the armed services and appropriations committees.

options.text: No notice, because the HCA's multiyear determination already covers the cancellation ceiling and the funding plan
options.why: An agency determination does not replace the statutory congressional notice for large cancellation ceilings.

options.text: Notice 10 days before award, as for terminations
options.why: The 10-day notice in 10 U.S.C. 3501(l)(6) concerns termination of a multiyear contract, not award with a large cancellation ceiling.

options.text: Written notice to the armed services and appropriations committees of both houses, then no award for 31 days
options.why: For DoD, NASA and the Coast Guard, 17.104-3(b)-(c) applies to cancellation ceilings over $200 million; DFARS 217.104-370(b)(1)(iv) mirrors it.

stem: Before entering into a DoD multiyear contract for covered installation services under DFARS 217.103-171, what must the head of the agency determine in writing?

options.text: A stable design and a Secretary of Defense certification to Congress 30 days before award
options.why: Stable design and SecDef certification belong to multiyear supply contracts under 10 U.S.C. 3501, not services under 3531.

options.text: That each option year will be evaluated at award and exercised only if funds are available, with the total value of the options kept under the approved cancellation ceiling
options.why: That describes a multiple-year contract with options; a multiyear contract buys the program years without options.

options.text: A continuing need; substantial start-up investment or contingent liabilities for a special workforce; and that multiyear contracting helps competition and economy
options.why: These are the three determinations in DFARS 217.103-171(c), implementing 10 U.S.C. 3531(a).

options.text: That the contract is specifically authorized by law because it exceeds $900 million
options.why: Specific statutory authority is required only above $900 million; it is not a prerequisite for an $84 million services multiyear.

stem: An Army prototype Other Transaction is expected to cost $720 million including options. What approval and notice does 10 U.S.C. 4022 require?

options.text: A written determination by USD(A&S) or USD(R&E), with notice to the congressional defense committees 30 days before the authority is used
options.why: That was the rule before the FY2025 NDAA; section 816 moved the over-$500 million determination to the senior procurement executive.

options.text: A non-delegable SPE determination in writing, and written notice to the congressional defense committees 30 days before use
options.why: 4022(a)(2)(B), as amended by the FY2025 NDAA, applies this to prototype transactions over $500 million, and (a)(3) bars delegation.

options.text: A written determination by the head of the contracting activity
options.why: The HCA determination covers prototype transactions over $100 million up to $500 million.

options.text: A covered official's written determination, with notice to the congressional defense committees when the authority is exercised
options.why: That is the rule for follow-on production contracts or transactions over $100 million under 4022(a)(2)(C).

stem: An Army follow-on production transaction under 10 U.S.C. 4022(f) is expected to cost $1.4 billion. What approval and notice does the statute require?

options.text: A covered official's written determination that 4022(d) was met, 4022(f) will be met and the authority is essential to critical national security objectives, with notice to the committees when used
options.why: That is 4022(a)(2)(C) for follow-on production contracts or transactions over $100 million.

options.text: A senior procurement executive determination, plus notice to the congressional defense committees at least 30 days before the award is made
options.why: The 30-day advance notice applies to prototype transactions over $500 million under 4022(a)(2)(B), not to follow-on production.

options.text: No approval, because the prototype agreement already provided for follow-on production
options.why: Providing for follow-on production allows a noncompetitive award, but 4022(a)(2)(C) still requires the determination and notice above $100 million.

options.text: A new showing that a nontraditional defense contractor participates to a significant extent in the follow-on, approved by the HCA in writing, with notice to the congressional defense committees
options.why: Under 4022(d)(3) the participation conditions do not apply to the follow-on; the covered official finds they were met for the prototype transaction.

stem: Under Army Warranting Program Policy v12, which statement about an unlimited warrant is correct?

options.text: The HCA must attest to the candidate's superior judgment and decision-making, and the review board cannot be waived.
options.why: Section 4.3 states both requirements in those terms.

options.text: The HCA may waive the board with a written risk assessment and business case recorded in VCE-Warrants.
options.why: That general waiver in section 3.3 does not reach the unlimited-warrant board, which 4.3 says cannot be waived.

options.text: An unlimited warrant lets the holder sign before required approvals, such as a justification or acquisition plan approval, are obtained.
options.why: FAR 1.402-2(a)(1) requires all clearances and approvals before signing; the warrant sets dollar authority only.

options.text: A written test can substitute for the board for an unlimited warrant.
options.why: Section 4.3 requires successfully passing the appropriate warranting review board.

cite: Army Warranting Program Policy v12 (MAR 2026) sec. 4.3

stem: A $1.3 billion cost-plus-incentive-fee services contract is negotiated, but ASA(ALT) has not yet approved the acquisition plan or the E.O. 14402 justification. The solicitation issued in May 2026 and funds expire in six days. What should the unlimited-warrant contracting officer do?

options.text: Not sign until the required approvals are obtained, push for expedited staffing, and give leadership a written status now.
options.why: FAR 1.402-2(a) requires all approvals before signing, and early notice lets leadership make funding decisions in time.

options.text: Sign by 30 September, because an unlimited warrant covers any dollar value, and obtain the approvals afterward.
options.why: The warrant sets dollar authority only; it does not replace approvals that belong to ASA(ALT).

options.text: Sign if the Commanding General gives the direction in writing.
options.why: A written direction does not supply missing approvals or relieve the contracting officer of FAR 1.402-2 responsibilities.

options.text: Sign, because the E.O. 14402 justification applies only to solicitations issued on or after 15 July 2026.
options.why: For solicitations issued before 15 July 2026 with award after that date, an approved justification is still required before award.

stem: As of September 2026, which statement about peer review of a $420 million sole-source DoD contract action is correct?

options.text: It gets a streamlined DPCAP peer review under the tiered process that implements the 4 May 2026 USW(A&S) memo.
options.why: The DPCAP memo sets a streamlined review for sole-source actions over $50 million and under $500 million.

options.text: No DoD-level review is required, because DPCAP noncompetitive peer reviews start at $1 billion.
options.why: That was the printed PGI threshold; the May 2026 memos brought sole-source actions over $50 million into DPCAP review.

options.text: It receives only a postaward Independent Management Review because it is under $500 million.
options.why: IMRs are Army postaward reviews of service contracts and do not replace preaward sole-source peer review.

options.text: Peer review applies only if the contractor's proposal, not the Government objective, exceeds $500 million.
options.why: PGI 201.170 uses the greater of the Government objective or the proposal, and the tiers start above $50 million.

cite: DPCAP memo USA001395-26 (implementing the 4 May 2026 USW(A&S) memo); DFARS PGI 201.170(a)(1)(ii)

stem: A DPCAP peer review team labels a recommendation significant on a $2.4 billion competitive MDAP acquisition. The contracting officer does not intend to follow it. What must happen?

options.text: The contracting activity's senior procurement official must be told before the contracting officer acts against it.
options.why: PGI 201.170-3(a) makes that awareness the condition for departing from a significant recommendation.

options.text: The contracting officer must follow it, because significant recommendations are binding on the whole contracting activity.
options.why: PGI 201.170-3(a) says peer review results are advisory and preserve the contracting officer's judgment.

options.text: USD(A&S) must approve the departure in writing before award, after the peer review team briefs the issue to that office.
options.why: The PGI requires awareness by the contracting activity's senior procurement official, not USD(A&S) approval, briefed or not.

options.text: The contracting officer may proceed and raise the issue at the next scheduled review, with a note in the contract file.
options.why: The senior procurement official must be made aware before the contrary action is taken, not afterward.

cite: DFARS PGI 201.170-3(a)

stem: Who approves the written acquisition plan for a $700 million Army services acquisition that is not managed by a PAE or DRPM?

options.text: DASA(P), under delegation from ASA(ALT), with no power to delegate further.
options.why: Appendix GG places the $500 million to under $1 billion tier at DASA(P) without further delegation.

options.text: The HCA, delegable no lower than the SCO.
options.why: That tier applies to non-PAE acquisitions below $500 million.

options.text: ASA(ALT), not delegable.
options.why: That tier applies at $1 billion or more, or to special interest acquisitions.

options.text: No one, because firm-fixed-price services do not need a written plan.
options.why: DFARS 207.103-70(a) requires a written plan for services of $50 million or more regardless of contract type.

stem: Which approval level applies to the services acquisition strategy for a $1.4 billion Army services requirement?

options.text: The Army Acquisition Executive, delegable only to DASA(P) or the Senior Services Manager.
options.why: Appendix GG places Category I services ($1 billion or more, or more than $300 million in a year) at that level.

options.text: The HCA, delegable no lower than the SCO.
options.why: That is the Category III tier, for $100 million to under $250 million.

options.text: The HCA, delegable no lower than the chief of the contracting office.
options.why: That is the Category IV tier, for $10 million to under $100 million.

options.text: USD(A&S), because every services acquisition over $1 billion is automatically special interest.
options.why: Special interest designation is a separate decision, not automatic at $1 billion.

stem: An Army contracting officer will award a $1.1 billion contract. Which statement about the public announcement is correct?

options.text: Send it to ODASA(P) by noon Eastern three business days before award, and release nothing before 5 p.m. Eastern on award day.
options.why: AFARS PGI 5105.302(a) sets the Army lead time, and FAR 5.302(a) sets the 5 p.m. release rule.

options.text: The Commanding General may announce the awardee at a morning event on award day if the contract was signed and distributed that morning.
options.why: FAR 5.302(a) bars release of award information before 5 p.m. Eastern.

options.text: DoD announces only awards over $5.5 million, counting all unexercised options in the value, and ODASA(P) is told on the day of award.
options.why: The DoD threshold is $9 million, and face value excludes unexercised options (DFARS 205.302(a)(i)); the Army also needs the announcement three business days ahead.

options.text: The SCO may authorize award before ODASA(P) approval whenever the schedule is at risk.
options.why: The only Army exception is an urgency award with DASA(P) written approval, and no contracting-activity deviation is allowed.

stem: A contractor has material weaknesses in both its estimating and purchasing systems. Under DFARS 252.242-7998, what is the maximum total withhold on each progress payment or interim voucher under a covered contract?

options.text: 10 percent
options.why: Paragraph (e)(3) caps withholding at 10 percent for material weaknesses in multiple business systems.

options.text: 5 percent
options.why: Five percent is the cap for weaknesses in a single business system.

options.text: 2 percent
options.why: Two percent is the reduced rate once an acceptable corrective action plan is being effectively implemented.

options.text: 30 percent, which is 5 percent for each of the six business systems
options.why: The clause caps total withholding at 10 percent no matter how many systems have weaknesses.

stem: A contractor's estimating system was disapproved for material weaknesses. The contractor asks the PCO on another covered contract to stop the withhold because of cash flow. What is the correct response?

options.text: Refer it to the contracting officer who made the final determination; release depends on an acceptable plan or verified correction.
options.why: DFARS 242.7000(b)-(d) and 252.242-7998(e)-(f) give that contracting officer control of the withhold and set the release conditions.

options.text: The PCO may stop the withhold on the PCO's own contract if performance is at risk and the PCO documents the contractor's cash flow problem.
options.why: The clause ties reductions and release to corrective action and verification, not to a PCO's schedule or cash flow concerns.

options.text: The withhold must continue unchanged until DCAA completes a full follow-up audit.
options.why: The rules allow a reduction to 2 percent under an effectively implemented plan and early release on a reasonable expectation of correction.

options.text: The contractor may stop withholding on its interim vouchers as soon as it submits any corrective action plan to the contracting officer for review.
options.why: Only an acceptable plan that the contracting officer finds is being effectively implemented reduces the withhold, and only to 2 percent.

stem: On a DoD cost-plus-award-fee contract, the program wants only 20 percent of the award fee available for the final evaluation. What is required?

options.text: A contracting officer determination plus the HCA's personal approval, which cannot be delegated.
options.why: DFARS 216.402-470(a) sets a 40 percent floor that only the HCA, personally, can lower.

options.text: Nothing, because the fee-determining official decides how the award fee pool is allocated across the evaluation periods.
options.why: Approving the plan does not reach the 40 percent floor; going below it needs a contracting officer determination and HCA approval that cannot be delegated.

options.text: It is prohibited in all cases, because at least 40 percent must stay available for the final evaluation.
options.why: The 40 percent floor is real, but it can be lowered with non-delegable HCA approval.

options.text: Approval by the SCO under the award-fee D&F delegation, after the contracting officer's determination.
options.why: The D&F delegation does not reach the 40 percent rule, which requires the HCA personally.

stem: Under the RFO FAR, a contractor's overall cost, schedule and technical performance for an award-fee period is below satisfactory in the aggregate. Which action is correct?

options.text: Award no fee for the period, document why, and do not roll the unearned fee forward.
options.why: FAR 16.402-2(c) and (d)(5) bar earning fee below satisfactory, and 16.402-2(e) prohibits rollover.

options.text: Award up to 50 percent, because some technical criteria were exceeded during the period.
options.why: Up to 50 percent is the Satisfactory band, which requires meeting overall requirements in the aggregate.

options.text: Move the unearned fee into the final evaluation period to keep the contractor motivated.
options.why: FAR 16.402-2(e) prohibits rollover of unearned award fee.

options.text: Pay the fee now but reduce the next period's pool by the same amount.
options.why: No fee can be earned below satisfactory, and an offset against a future pool does not change that.

stem: A losing offeror challenges the evaluation on a $62 million DoD task order under a multiple-award contract. Where may it protest?

options.text: Only at GAO, because the order is over $35 million
options.why: FAR 16.508(b) and 10 U.S.C. 3406(f)(2) limit protests of DoD orders over $35 million to GAO.

options.text: At GAO or the Court of Federal Claims, at the protester's choice
options.why: The Court of Federal Claims cannot hear DoD order protests except on scope, period or maximum-value grounds.

options.text: Nowhere, because task orders cannot be protested
options.why: DoD orders over $35 million are protestable at GAO.

options.text: Only at the agency, because the order is under $100 million
options.why: No $100 million agency-only rule exists; the DoD threshold is $35 million and the forum is GAO.

stem: Who may authorize continued performance of a $240 million DoD task order after a timely GAO protest triggers the stay?

options.text: The HCA, nondelegably, after a written finding and notice to GAO
options.why: FAR 33.105-3(b)(2)-(c) and 31 U.S.C. 3553(d)(3)(C) and (e) name that official and require the finding and the notice.

options.text: The contracting officer, with legal concurrence and a written finding
options.why: The contracting officer cannot override the stay, even with a finding; the statute reserves it to the head of the procuring activity.

options.text: The SCO, if the HCA delegates the authority in writing for this order
options.why: 31 U.S.C. 3553(e) and Appendix GG make the override authority nondelegable.

options.text: No one; performance may not resume until GAO decides the protest
options.why: The HCA may override with a written best-interests or urgent-and-compelling finding.

stem: A contracting officer wants to use cost-plus-fixed-fee for a noncommercial $40 million services requirement. Under FAR 16.301-3(a), which condition must be met?

options.text: The written acquisition plan has been approved at least one level above the contracting officer.
options.why: FAR 16.301-3(a)(1) lists that approval as a condition.

options.text: The contractor has an approved purchasing system.
options.why: FAR 16.301-3(a)(3) requires an adequate accounting system, not an approved purchasing system.

options.text: The head of the agency has approved an E.O. 14402 justification.
options.why: That justification is required only when FAR 16.104 applies, which for DoD starts at $100 million.

options.text: The SCO has signed a determination and findings for the contract type before the solicitation is issued.
options.why: A D&F is required for incentive and award-fee contracts (16.401-2), not as a general cost-reimbursement condition, whenever it is signed.

stem: Which Army action requires an Executive Order 14402 justification under FAR 16.104?

options.text: A $180 million time-and-materials task order under a multiple-award IDIQ
options.why: Multiple-award contracts are exempt, but covered orders under them at $100 million or more still need a justification.

options.text: A $90 million cost-plus-fixed-fee services contract
options.why: The DoD threshold is $100 million.

options.text: A $400 million firm-fixed-price production contract
options.why: Firm-fixed-price contracts, other than level-of-effort term, are not covered.

options.text: A $250 million cost-plus-fixed-fee contract supporting a contingency operation
options.why: Contracts supporting an emergency, major disaster or contingency operation are excepted by 16.104(e)(2).

stem: A DoD contractor with a valid FPRA proposes different rates on a sole-source modification. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The PCO uses the FPRA rates unless the HCA or a designee waives them here, and tells the ACO about changed conditions.
options.why: FAR 15.405-3(b) and DFARS 215.405-3(b) require FPRA rates unless waived case by case, with changed conditions sent to the ACO.

options.text: The PCO may renegotiate the FPRA rates for this modification.
options.why: FAR 42.302(a)(5) makes FPRA negotiation a function of the cognizant Federal agency, performed by the ACO.

options.text: The contractor must sign a certificate of current cost or pricing data when the FPRA is agreed, covering the newly proposed rates.
options.why: FAR 15.405-3(c) bars requiring certification at FPRA agreement; the certificate for the pricing action covers the data.

options.text: FPRA rates are advisory, so the PCO may use any rate between the proposed rate and the FPRA rate if the file explains why.
options.why: DFARS 215.405-3(b) requires using FPRA rates when available unless they are waived; an explanation in the file is not a waiver.

stem: On a DoD sole-source proposal, when does DFARS PGI 215.406 say the contracting officer should consider requesting DCAA audit assistance?

options.text: For fixed-price proposals over $10 million or cost-type proposals over $100 million
options.why: PGI 215.406(b)(1) sets those two audit-assistance thresholds.

options.text: For any proposal above the simplified acquisition threshold
options.why: PGI 215.406(b)(2) says not to request DCAA audit below the stated amounts absent exceptional circumstances.

options.text: Only for cost-type proposals, since fixed-price risk sits with the contractor
options.why: Fixed-price proposals over $10 million are a listed audit-assistance case.

options.text: Only when the contractor has a material weakness in a business system
options.why: Material weaknesses affect the field pricing thresholds for cost-type proposals; the DCAA audit thresholds are dollar-based.
